articles.title: Trump tells Cohen he was ‘weaponized’ in feud
articles.summary: President Trump suggested Michael Cohen was “forced” to testify against him in the 2024 New York hush money trial in a Thursday clip from the president’s upcoming interview with his former personal attorney. “They weaponized government against you and against others, Michael. There were plenty of others too, and it’s a disgrace,” the president told…
articles.body:
President Trump suggested Michael Cohen was “forced” to testify against him in the 2024 New York hush money trial in a Thursday clip from the president’s upcoming interview with his former personal attorney.

“They weaponized government against you and against others, Michael. There were plenty of others too, and it’s a disgrace,” the president told Cohen. “I think it’s so amazing that you came out, and you told the story, and people respect you for doing it.”

The conversation, which will air in full on Cohen’s 77 WABC radio show on Sunday, follows years of public acrimony between the pair.

The feud between the president and his personal lawyer stemmed from Cohen’s 2018 guilty plea in Manhattan federal court to eight criminal counts in a payment scheme created to silence women who claimed to have had affairs with Trump.

Cohen later served as a star witness in Trump’s New York hush money criminal trial, in which the president was convicted in 2024 on 34 counts of falsifying business records connected to payments to adult film actor Stormy Daniels.

Earlier this year, the lawyer claimed he was pressured by New York Attorney General Letitia James and Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg to testify against his former client in this case.

“I felt compelled and coerced to deliver what they were seeking,” Cohen wrote in a Substack post . “Letitia James and Alvin Bragg may not share the same office, but they share the same playbook.”

In other segments of their conversation shared by WABC on Thursday, the president defended his administration’s military operations in Iran and pushed back on unfavorable approval ratings.

“I think that we’re doing really well in the polls — the real polls,” Trump said. “If I were running today, I think I’d win by 25 points. I think we’d win by a lot.”

Cohen described his relationship with Trump as being “resuscitated” in an interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper ahead of the clip’s release on Thursday evening.

“I truly believe that there is forgiveness between Donald Trump and myself, and that to me is what is important right now,” the attorney said.

Cohen told CNN that he has submitted a pardon application during Trump’s second term, but that he has not asked the president directly about this request. The attorney said he has not received a notice that the White House has received his application and intends to follow up on Friday.

articles.title: Melania Trump jokes about her low profile in Rose Garden remarks
articles.summary: First lady Melania Trump poked fun at her low profile throughout her husband’s second term during a White House event Thursday, making her first major public appearance since mid-July. “Good afternoon,” the first lady greeted press at the White House Rose Garden for an event highlighting her new foster care scholarship initiative. “I heard you…
articles.body:
First lady Melania Trump poked fun at her low profile throughout her husband’s second term during a White House event Thursday, making her first major public appearance since mid-July.

“Good afternoon,” the first lady greeted press at the White House Rose Garden for an event highlighting her new foster care scholarship initiative. “I heard you missed me. Here I am.”

The first lady has not played a prominent role in the second Trump administration, often staying out of the national spotlight. But she took the stage Thursday to announce a new round of scholarships for foster children, in partnership with Fox Corporation and IndyCar — ahead of its upcoming Freedom 250 Grand Prix.

Prior to the president’s second inauguration, Melania Trump said in an interview she thought getting used to life at the White House would be easier than during her husband’s first term.

articles.title: Markey, Moulton lock horns ahead of Massachusetts Senate primary: 3 takeaways from last debate
articles.summary: Rep. Seth Moulton and Sen. Ed Markey exchanged blows from the onset of the final Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary debate as the 47-year-old House lawmaker mounts a long-shot bid to oust his 80-year-old progressive opponent. Moulton and Markey appeared for their last televised debate on Thursday, which was hosted by WCVB-TV, WBUR-FM and The Boston…
articles.body:
Rep. Seth Moulton and Sen. Ed Markey exchanged blows from the onset of the final Massachusetts Democratic Senate primary debate as the 47-year-old House lawmaker mounts a long-shot bid to oust his 80-year-old progressive opponent.

Moulton and Markey appeared for their last televised debate on Thursday, which was hosted by WCVB-TV, WBUR-FM and The Boston Globe in Boston, ahead of the Sept. 1 primary. Early voting begins Saturday.

Moulton has framed the race around generational change while questioning Markey’s progressive bona fides. He’s suggested the Massachusetts senator has not done enough to fight back against the Trump administration and advance priorities like the Green New Deal.

Meanwhile, Markey scoffed at the attacks, pointing to his central role in authoring the climate-oriented policy while seeking to tie the congressman to past votes and statements on everything from the Iran war to transgender rights. He also noted that he received endorsements from key progressives including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.).

Polling has consistently shown Markey comfortably leading Moulton in the contest. The winner of the September primary will be the heavy favorite to win the Senate seat in the Bay State come November.

Here are the key takeaways from Thursday’s debate:

Moulton touts progressive positions while his moderate preferences peek through

Throughout the race, Moulton, who has made his brand as a more left-of-center Democrat in the House, has sought to position himself as the more progressive of the two in the Senate primary. That theme was on clear display during their final debate, though he didn’t shy away several times from highlighting more moderate Democrats or leaning toward more moderated stances.

When asked during the debate what democratic socialist candidates were getting right or wrong, the House Democrat applauded their focus on affordability, mentioning New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani before citing centrist Govs. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey. The two governors who won their elections in 2025, and they are more moderate Democrats and not democratic socialists.

“I have put forward such a progressive affordability agenda that plants the flag in the ground and says that housing, healthcare and education should be human rights,” Moulton said.

Markey, meanwhile, regularly touted his left-wing support, including endorsements from Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.).

“Our party has to become more progressive,” Markey said. “We have to stand up for what the people are talking about at the grassroots, especially young people.”

“They support Medicare for All. They know the healthcare system in our country is a sick care system. They want it fixed. They want a Green New Deal,” he continued. “They want to take what I’ve already led on, and they want to build it even bigger.”

During a discussion over whether transgender athletes should be allowed to play in the sport that aligns with their gender, Moulton said they should, with the caveat that there should be a “discussion” that touches on “issues of safety and fairness.”

Markey is one of the oldest senators in the upper chamber, and Moulton has made his opponent’s age and generational change focal points in his Senate pitch.

“I’m running against the senator’s decision after 50 years in Washington, to run for another term at age 80,” the congressman said in his closing remarks. “I believe in a new generation of leadership. I believe we can do better than the status quo.”

Moulton reiterated his support for age limits in Congress, while Markey said that if a lawmaker “can’t do the job, they should just step down.”

On Thursday’s debate stage, Moulton jabbed at Markey’s response to a question about whether he used AI platforms in his work. The senator said he used “whatever is inside of my iPhone and my iPad,” while noting he didn’t know which companies his iPad could be using.

“With all due respect, senator, if you don’t even know what you’re using on your phone or your iPad, like, this is why we need a new generation of leaders to regulate these technologies,” Moulton retorted.

But Markey has maintained he’s still up for the job and that Moulton has “a hard time keeping up” with him on the campaign trail. He also accused the congressman of discovering issues while campaigning for the Senate, whereas the senator said he was leading on them already in the upper chamber.

“I’m more energized than I’ve ever been before,” he said Thursday, noting that he was “crisscrossing the state” and “fighting for families.”

Responding to Moulton’s attack regarding the AI platforms he was using, the senator said the name of the application didn’t matter.

“We need to build safeguards around it, and that is what my legislation is accomplishing,” Markey said.

Markey zeroes in on Moulton over trans rights

During the debate, the senator renewed his attacks on Moulton over his 2024 remarks on transgender girls and women being allowed to play in sports aligned with their gender — comments Moulton has since apologized for and tried to walk back.

“Congressman Moulton threw those kids under the political bus after the election of 2024. He just turned them into political fodder that made them afraid. We should have been loving those kids,” Markey said.

The congressman said shortly after the 2024 election that he opposed transgender girls and women playing on sports teams that align with their gender.

“Democrats spend way too much time trying not to offend anyone rather than being brutally honest about the challenges many Americans face,” Moulton told The New York Times in an interview at the time. “I have two little girls, I don’t want them getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete, but as a Democrat I’m supposed to be afraid to say that.”

The congressman has voted for and even co-sponsored legislation that aims to support the transgender community, such as House Democrats’ Transgender Bill of Rights.

Moulton has since apologized for his comments.

“To anyone hurt by my comments, I’m sorry because that was not my intention,” he said Thursday. “My intention was to say that we need to take on these issues.”

While Moulton supported the right of transgender girls and women to play on teams that align with their gender, he still suggested there should be a “discussion” and argued Democrats shouldn’t be ceding the issue to Republicans.

articles.title: Democrats urge ICE to halt purchase of electric gloves ‘before more innocent lives are lost’
articles.summary: House Democrats on the Homeland Security Committee are calling for Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin to abandon plans to equip immigration agents with electric shock gloves and “halt this procurement before more innocent lives are lost.” U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) earlier this month published a notice of their plan to…
articles.body:
House Democrats on the Homeland Security Committee are calling for Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin to abandon plans to equip immigration agents with electric shock gloves and “halt this procurement before more innocent lives are lost.”

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) earlier this month published a notice of their plan to buy the generated low output voltage emitter, marketed as G.L.O.V.E., prompting widespread concern over how they may be used. ICE is a part of DHS led by Mullin.

“Under the Trump administration, ICE has repeatedly violated the law and disregarded its own policies on the use of force, shooting 23 people and killing 6, including 3 U.S. citizens. Many of these individuals were not the target of immigration enforcement operations and, in some cases, they were simply exercising their First Amendment rights. As we have raised in previous letters, DHS personnel have also permanently injured and nearly killed innocent people with so-called ‘less-lethal’ weapons, not unlike the G.L.O.V.E.,” Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.) wrote in the letter to Mullin.

“Indeed, ICE has demonstrated a pattern of misusing tools and devices, including rubber bullets and chemical sprays, in manners that put the public at greater risk of serious injury or death.”

In addition to the high-profile killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, who both died in altercations with federal agents in Minnesota, the use of rubber bullets by federal law enforcement has led to several protestors being blinded in one eye .

Guidance from the company that produces the gloves, Compliant Technologies, recommends various limitations in its own literature, noting that failure to follow guidelines could result in “ injury or death .”

The product manual for G.L.O.V.E. outlines a number of potential dangers with the product, including advising that it not be used against the elderly, pregnant or disabled people while noting that not all underlying medical conditions are visible.

Thompson noted that the gloves should not be used on one individual by two officers at the same time and that the company advises against skin contact beyond 15 seconds.

“Given ICE’s horrific record of violence against the public, the agency must not be allowed to equip its officers and agents with a device that demands both significant training for and restraint by its users,” Thompson said.

The Trump administration has defended its plans to purchase the gloves, thought it has not said when officers might receive them or in what setting they might be used, such as within detention facilities rather than with the broader public.

In response to The Hill, DHS repeated the same statement it has previously issues about the gloves.

“ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country. Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards,” a DHS spokesperson said.

Border czar Tom Homan has described the gloves as something of an intermediary step.

“Look, it’s another device to help someone be compliant, whether or not — you know, you just can’t go from zero to 100, right?” he said during an appearance on Fox News last week.

“There’s a lot of training involved. There’s still some background issues that need to be dealt with. So, the implementation of these gloves out in the field are going to be a while. I think they serve a better purpose in detention facility, where detainees get out of control and there’s fights in the facility,” Homan said.

“So we’ll see. Still, the training protocol is being written and being reviewed. Then we’ll see when they get rolled out.”

articles.title: Trump seeks to boost Darline Graham in South Carolina homestretch
articles.summary: President Trump is seeking to give Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) a final boost as her candidacy hits a road bump in the race to replace her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.). Trump will hit the campaign trail Friday for Darline Graham, whom he appointed to fill out her brother’s term, ahead of her…
articles.body:
President Trump is seeking to give Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) a final boost as her candidacy hits a road bump in the race to replace her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

Trump will hit the campaign trail Friday for Darline Graham, whom he appointed to fill out her brother’s term, ahead of her runoff election in the GOP primary Tuesday against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.).

The race will stand as a test for the strength of Trump’s endorsement as Graham, a political novice, enters the arena.

Her inexperience was on full display on the debate stage Tuesday, when she flubbed a national security question, drawing attacks on her fitness to serve in the Senate.

Trump and Graham are slated to campaign in Myrtle Beach, which is home to former Senate candidate Rep. Russell Fry’s (R-S.C.) district. Fry lost his bid for Senate in the initial Republican primary election to replace Graham and did not advance, making his support base critical for Norman and Graham.

“Myrtle Beach is the exact correct place for them to go. It is the heart of Russell Fry’s district and home to probably the largest population of persuadable voters that we expect will be voting,” said Mick Mulvaney, who served in Trump’s first administration and represented South Carolina’s 5th Congressional District in the House.

“Trump will obviously carry a lot of weight. But how much remains to be seen. Polling indicates that maybe only 40 percent of voters put a lot of weight on his endorsement,” he continued.

“That, combined with her astonishingly poor performance in the debate earlier this week, may make this race much closer than people realize,” he said.

During her primary debate against Norman on Tuesday, Graham was asked how Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues. Graham admitted “national security is not” her thing but that she supports the military.

The answer marked a stark contrast between her and her late brother, who was seen as a key foreign policy leader in the Senate. It was also met with immediate criticism from Norman and his allies.

“Lindsey Graham was well informed on the United States’ national security. Darline Graham admits she’s not. This is not something you inherit. And it’s critical in the U.S. Senate,” former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley, who ran against Trump in 2024 and is supporting Norman, said in a post on X.

Norman told Kellie Meyer of NewsNation that Graham’s debate response was “serious.”

“What is more serious is who she is getting supported by is everything I’m against,” he added.

Graham sought to clean up the comment during a sit-down interview on Fox News’s “Hannity” Wednesday, casting herself at the opposite of a career politician.

“I have said many times I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician,” Graham said.

Maggie Knox, a South Carolina GOP official who is not endorsing in the primary, characterized Graham’s answer as “an honest response.”

“Could she have answered that better? Absolutely,” Knox told The Hill. “I had breakfast with someone this morning and she said, ‘I liked it that she didn’t pretend like she knew something she didn’t. That was kind of refreshing.’”

Graham walks into Tuesday with an advantage from Trump’s endorsement and her status as Lindsey Graham’s sister. Trump won the state by nearly 18 points in 2024, by 11 points in 2020, and by 14 points in 2016.

“Without Trump, Darline wouldn’t have a chance,” Mulvaney said. “And by that, I mean she’d be polling at very low, single digits.”

A source with Graham’s campaign told The Hill that her team is relying on more than just the president’s backing to get across the finish line.

“It opens a door, but it doesn’t walk you through it,” the source said, referring to Trump’s endorsement as “the gold standard” in politics.

“People want to know that their candidate is going to work with President Trump, and that’s as, if not more, important than the endorsement,” the source said, citing Graham’s work since being appointed to the Senate by Trump.

While Trump’s endorsement is objectively helpful, he does not have a perfect record in this cycle.

Earlier this week, Trump took losses when Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.) lost his primary race, as well as his endorsed candidate for Florida’s 19th Congressional District.

Rep. Andy Ogles (R), who was backed by Trump, also lost his primary in Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District along with Rep. Randy Feenstra (R) in Iowa’s gubernatorial primary and Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones (R) in Georgia’s gubernatorial primary.

Trump issued a rare double endorsement of South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson (R) and Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette (R) in June after Evette, his initial pick, failed to avoid a runoff election and later lost.

While Norman has supported Trump’s second administration, he notably endorsed Haley over Trump for president in 2024. Additionally, as a member of the fiscally conservative House Freedom Caucus, Norman and his colleagues have not been afraid to push back on the administration and House Republican leadership.

The source with Graham’s campaign argued that Norman would be “a caucus of one” and does not want to work with the president.

Norman told NewsNation his support for Trump is “unwavering.”

“Do I need a call? No. I’ll support him regardless because I believe in what he’s doing,” the congressman said.

“The Senate has been the graveyard for every good thing [Trump] wants,” he said, adding that like Trump, he would like to “blow up” the filibuster.

The winner of Tuesday’s runoff will go on to face Democratic candidate Annie Andrews in November.

“I think a lot of South Carolinians are looking at this and thinking who is more likely able to go against Annie Andrews and come out on top,” Knox said.

Andrews faces an uphill climb in the red state. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the race as solid Republican. However, nationally Republicans are facing headwinds amid Trump’s declining approval ratings and rising Democratic enthusiasm.

Trump’s approval rating in South Carolina sits at 42 percent, according to a Civiqs tracking poll .

“We know that this is a tough midterm. We know that we are up against a voting public that is certainly battling some voter fatigue, and we are trying to energize our party but it’s a tough row to hoe, I’m not going to lie,” Knox said.

“Are we super worried about Annie Andrews? No, but are we going to play it like we have it in the bag? Absolutely not,” she said.

A source with Graham’s campaign told The Hill that her team is relying on more than just the president’s backing to get across the finish line.
“It opens a door, but it doesn’t walk you through it,” the source said, referring to Trump’s endorsement as “the gold standard” in politics.

“People want to know that their candidate is going to work with President Trump, and that’s as, if not more, important than the endorsement,” the source said, citing Graham’s work since being appointed to the Senate by Trump.
While Trump’s endorsement is objectively helpful, he does not have a perfect record in this cycle.
Earlier this week, Trump took losses when Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.) lost his primary race, as well as his endorsed candidate for Florida’s 19th Congressional District.

Rep. Andy Ogles (R), who was backed by Trump, also lost his primary in Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District along with Rep. Randy Feenstra (R) in Iowa’s gubernatorial primary and Georgia Lt. Gov. Burt Jones (R) in Georgia’s gubernatorial primary.

Trump issued a rare double endorsement of South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson (R) and Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette (R) in June after Evette, his initial pick, failed to avoid a runoff election and later lost.

While Norman has supported Trump’s second administration, he notably endorsed Haley over Trump for president in 2024. Additionally, as a member of the fiscally conservative House Freedom Caucus, Norman and his colleagues have not been afraid to push back on the administration and House Republican leadership.
The source with Graham’s campaign argued that Norman would be “a caucus of one” and does not want to work with the president.
Norman told NewsNation his support for Trump is “unwavering.”
“Do I need a call? No. I’ll support him regardless because I believe in what he’s doing,” the congressman said.
“The Senate has been the graveyard for every good thing [Trump] wants,” he said, adding that like Trump, he would like to “blow up” the filibuster.
The winner of Tuesday’s runoff will go on to face Democratic candidate Annie Andrews in November.

Trump’s approval rating in South Carolina sits at 42 percent, according to a Civiqs tracking poll .

“We know that this is a tough midterm. We know that we are up against a voting public that is certainly battling some voter fatigue, and we are trying to energize our party but it’s a tough row to hoe, I’m not going to lie,” Knox said.

articles.title: Gen Z turns against capitalism as DSA takes off
articles.summary: Only 9 percent of Americans younger than 30 have a “very positive” view of capitalism, according to a new CBS/YouGov poll. That shows a stark generation between Generation Z and older generations. Thirty-three percent of people older than 65, or those in the baby boomer generation, said they have a very positive view of capitalism, while…
articles.body:
Only 9 percent of Americans younger than 30 have a “very positive” view of capitalism, according to a new CBS/YouGov poll .

That shows a stark generation between Generation Z and older generations.

Thirty-three percent of people older than 65, or those in the baby boomer generation, said they have a very positive view of capitalism, while 23 percent of people aged 45-64, a group that includes Generation Xers and older millennials, view capitalism very positively.

Millennials in the 30-44 age range were closer to Gen Z, with just 15 percent saying they had a very positive view of capitalism.

Forty-one percent of respondents younger than 30 had a very negative or somewhat negative view of capitalism. That compares with 27 percent of those 65 and older, 32 percent of those aged 45-64 and 37 percent of those aged 30-44.

The data arrives amid a surge in democratic socialist victories across the U.S. — and not just in progressive corners of the country. Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon (D) on Tuesday beat out the more moderate Alex Vindman (D) in the Democratic Senate primary in Florida, a state known for its sunshine, not socialism.

Ashik Siddique, national co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), said the polling illustrates what the group is seeing at the street level: Generation Z is ready for a big change.

“We’ve seen that polling and it’s definitely striking, but to us, it really tracks with the experience that so many younger people have,” Siddique told The Hill.

“Gen Z, especially by now, just like wasn’t even raised with a lot of the assumptions that I think millennials were,” he added. “Seeing the condition of the world today, our government spending so much money on militarism and expanding ICE and giving tax cuts to the billionaires to the tune of trillions of dollars while public services are being cut for most Americans — it’s just like the contrast is really clear.”

When asked if there’s a gap between disliking capitalism and desiring a socialist economic system, Siddique said that in response to the capitalist status quo, “people are way more open to socialism.”

He cited a 2025 poll from Jacobin and the DSA Fund that found “Democrats prefer democratic socialism to capitalism by a 58-point margin.”

Nixon is seen as the underdog in the general election battle this fall.

In response to her primary win, election handicapper Sabato Crystal Ball shifted its projection for the seat from “likely Republican” to a safe Republican seat.

That’s partly because of the fundraising shortage Nixon is expected to have, but it also reflects doubts that democratic socialism will be a winning message in the fall in Florida.

CBS/YouGov interviewed 2,287 U.S. adults between August 12 and 14 for their poll, which had a 2.6-point margin of error.

Split up: Gen Z is the generation most divided by gender

Gen Z is the generation most politically split by gender, and the difference could affect the midterms this November.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris won 63 percent of women and 46 percent of men aged 18-29 in 2024, per a Catalist analysis . The 17-point gap was the largest of all generations, and also the largest Catalist has measured across four election cycles.

Tufts University’s Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) looked at ideological malleability in July and found that two-thirds of young adults have shifted their political views in recent years.

CIRCLE reported that 40 percent of young women said their beliefs remained unchanged, compared with 26 percent of young men. Among female respondents, 31 percent shifted to the left, 9 percent to the right, 11 percent to the center and 9 percent reported “other.”

Among male respondents, 22 percent shifted to the left, 21 percent to the right, 16 percent to the center and 14 percent reported “other.”

“Party is a really big driver of whether someone shows up to the ballot box,” Sara Suzuki, a senior researcher at CIRCLE, told The Hill. And across male- and female-identifying respondents — and probably most Americans — cost of living is a top concern. These factors could push people to the polls in November.

A June Economist/YouGov poll pinned President Trump’s approval rating among adults 18-29 at minus 45, the lowest it’s been in his presidency.

This dissatisfaction, alongside historical trends that show midterm election results serve as a reaction to who is in the White House, could mean that November may favor Democrats among Gen Z voters, according to Melissa Deckman, CEO of the Public Religion Research Institute.

Deckman added that young women are the most progressive age group and tend to lean left compared with their male counterparts. But this drastic difference between the two groups is unique to Gen Z, and it may be due to today’s media landscape.

“Gen Z has grown up in a fragmented media culture, and algorithms send young women and young men to different sites,” Deckman told The Hill.

This was evident in 2024, when Harris appeared on Alex Cooper’s “Call Her Daddy,” a podcast with a mostly female audience, and Trump spoke with Joe Rogan, Theo Von and NELK, to mostly male audiences .

November will hold several close races, but if any candidate can appeal across the Gen Z gender divide and pull across the aisle, they may have a better chance. “Young people go to the spheres they already belong to,” Suzuki said.

The CIRCLE study had a margin of error of 2.5 points and surveyed 5,549 adults between the ages 18 and 29

Cashing out: Is Gen Z opting for sports betting as a form of investing?

Some Gen Zers appear to be using sports betting platforms as an investment strategy.

The legalization and growing accessibility of sports betting has made it easier than ever to download sportsbooks like DraftKings, FanDuel and BetMGM, alongside prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket.

Sports betting has expanded from a $400 million industry in 2018 into a nearly $17 billion industry in 2026, and a large slice of that is Gen Z.

According to a survey from personal finance platform Betterment, 52 percent of Gen Z sports bettors are putting money intended for investing into sportsbooks, a 21-percentage point lead over millennials and 42-percentage point lead over Gen Xers.

Betterment’s survey was conducted between March 27 and April 3, 2026, interviewing a total of 1,000 U.S. respondents evenly split between Gen Z, millennials, Gen X and boomers.

About 1 in 8 investors say sports betting is part of their long-term investment strategy, which includes 26 percent of Gen Z. Thirty-six percent of Gen Z doesn’t participate in sports betting at all.

The reason why a large chunk of Gen Z is locked in on betting as an investment strategy is that young adults want a way to accelerate money made for long-term investing, or a “shortcut,” as CNBC calls it .

The National Council on Problem Gambling (NCPG) has identified trends in advertising, accessibility and Gen Z’s “hustle culture” that keep the generation hooked on making bets.

“When it comes to sports betting, the key items we’re identifying is responsiveness to advertising participation by mobile devices,” said Julia Brunson, communications manager for the NCPG.

“Sports betting is gambling, it’s not investing, and our position is that sports betting should only be done as entertainment, not as a strategy for making money or building wealth,” Brunson continued.

Brunson points out that Gen Z’s fixation on sports betting will most likely have an impact on Generation Alpha as well.

“[Gen Alpha] is currently interacting with sports betting products and prediction markets, they’re watching their older siblings do these things, they’re watching the games with them, you know, they’re engaging passively with advertising,” Brunson told The Hill.

Leaders in the sportsbook industry have also emphasized that placing money on sporting events is supposed to be fun, not an investment strategy.

“This is not confined to Gen Z or any other generation, sports betting is a form of entertainment,” a leader in the online gaming industry told The Hill. “It’s not a wealth creation vehicle, so the adults that decide to engage with wagering or gaming, or, you know, casino play, are doing this within a predetermined entertainment budget, and should not be doing it with money that is either needed for savings or for any other essential expense.”

In last week’s edition of The Feed, we reported on Gen Z’s growing reliance on and trust in crypto.

There’s a parallel between crypto and sports betting. In both cases, Gen Z is looking to easily accessible platforms to make some quick money or develop hobbies.

“All types of industries are trying to meet the small net with these generations that are basically born as digital natives, and so accessibility is an important component of that,” the online gaming industry leader said about the parallels sports betting has with other platforms.

Need support for gambling? Call or text 1-800-MY-RESET.

One last thing: The emojis you use may show your age 💯

You may be speaking a different language from people outside of your generation. That is, your emoji use might be aging you.

According to a study from The New York Times , different generations use different emojis for the same reaction. For example, 😭, 🤣 and 😂 were three of the most used emojis in 2025, but 😭 skyrocketed, particularly among teenage girls. In comparison, it was the least used among Gen X.

Although there are 24 other available heart emojis, Gen Alpha has adopted 🫰, and the symbol’s use has grown 109 percent in a year. (Look closely — the heart is at the cross in the fingers.)

The New York Times acquired the data from Reddit’s Academic Torrents , which published combined data from Pushshift and Arctic Shift by subreddit. Data was taken from November 2024 to January 2025 and November 2025 to January 2026.

Emoji use data was collected with Google’s Federated Analytics , capturing anonymous use of the GBoard (the default keyboard on stock Android devices like Google Pixel).

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com, jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com.

articles.title: Leaders can learn from Mike DeWine’s gravity-defying political career
articles.summary: Over a forty-nine year career marked by resilience and reelection to seven different offices, Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has shaped the state’s political landscape while emphasizing data-driven leadership and public service.
articles.body:
Here is an underreported story about a high-ranking official who has defied political gravity. Over the last 49 years, Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R), age 79, has been elected and reelected to seven prestigious county, state and federal offices. Despite two setbacks, he kept moving on and up.

DeWine won his first election as Greene County Prosecutor (1977 to 1981). He then served in the Ohio state Senate (1981 to 1982), the U.S. House of Representatives (1983 to 1991), as Ohio lieutenant governor (1991 to 1995), and in the U.S. Senate (1995 to 2007), where he lost his first bid in 1992 and was later defeated in 2006, while seeking his third term. Undeterred, DeWine was elected Ohio attorney general (serving from 2011 to 2019) and then governor (from January 2019 to until this coming January, term-limited).

Outside Ohio, DeWine is barely known, but his electoral record is unlikely to be matched by any politician. He shared his lessons, telling me, “My biggest regrets are when I didn’t have all the facts or didn’t drill down deep enough before making an informed decision.” The governor cautioned, “It is important to acknowledge that you aren’t always the expert, find the experts who can give you the data you need, and listen to those you want to lead and encourage them to come up with ideas.”

It remains unclear whether DeWine will be succeeded this November by Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy, whom he has endorsed, or by Democratic physician Amy Acton. Even in Ohio, where President Trump won by 11 points in 2024 , the political forecast is cloudy , with a chance of Republican defeat.

Moreover, the prospect of Republicans losing control of the Senate looms over a special election between Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D). DeWine has had his dealings with Brown, who walloped him in 2006 amid a tough year for Republicans nationwide and especially tough in Ohio .

This is a tangled saga. Then-Sen. Brown, running for his third term in 2024, was defeated by Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). Today, Brown is fighting to win the Senate seat previously held by Vice President JD Vance, which Gov. DeWine filled in January 2025 by appointing then-Lt. Gov. Husted.

DeWine is known for his resilience. After 12 years in the Senate, he returned to Ohio and taught government at several colleges before seeking elective office again. In 2010, he narrowly won the attorney general’s seat — an atypical post-Senate career move. He served under Gov. John Kasich (R).

After regaining his political momentum, Attorney General DeWine was overwhelmingly reelected in 2014. His work to test and develop criminal profiles from the massive backlog of rape-kits held by the state’s local law enforcement agencies — which laid bare the existence of 300 serial rapists in the state, who were linked to more than 1,100 crimes — helped propel him to his 2018 gubernatorial victory . Impressively, DeWine was reelected in 2022 by a 25-point margin.

Given DeWine’s remarkable journey through Washington and Ohio politics, he understands the fundamentals of leadership and governance. “Your mission and goals should always be clear and based on your core principles,” he explained. “Then, paint a picture of that vision so that people understand the ‘why’ behind it — why it’s important, why it matters, and why it will make a difference.”

DeWine emphasized, “You should be transparent and communicate what you know -and don’t know — focus on just a few big things, and then, be willing to make the tough decisions.”

That philosophy of focusing on “a few big things” is reflected in a recent stunning achievement; CNBC named Ohio “America’s top state for business 2026.” In his news release , DeWine stated, “When I took office, I promised to ‘plant the seeds’ of long-term investments that will positively impact Ohio for years to come. Today’s announcement is proof that these seeds are growing, and Ohio has a bright future ahead.”

After nearly five decades of continuous service, current and aspiring leaders can learn from Mike DeWine, a bespectacled, diminutive man who shuns the limelight. He is a workhorse who speaks truth to power , not a showhorse — the current political model.

When I asked Ann O’Donnell, the governor’s longtime chief advisor, how he managed to keep getting elected, she replied, “Mike DeWine is a radical optimist who believes deeply in the potential of all Ohioans. He loves Ohio and genuinely cares about the well-being of the people he has represented or governed.”

“Public service is both an incredible opportunity and an awesome responsibility,” DeWine told me. His advice to young officeholders: “Don’t waste time; treat every day you are in office with urgency while focusing on the things where you can make a difference.”

The governor also revealed his successful leadership style: “I taught my team a long time ago what we call the ‘but for’ test. But for you taking this action or that action, this change or the result would not have happened. If others are already doing it, then focus on something else.”

Regarding his remaining months in office, DeWine said, “I don’t spend much time thinking about legacy. Instead, I intend to help all Ohioans reach their full God-given potential.”

Summarizing her boss, chief advisor O’Donnell said, “He is the real deal, one of the last of a rare breed of public servants.”

Myra Adams served on the creative team of two Republican presidential campaigns in 2004 and 2008. Read more from her archive at The Hill.

The governor also revealed his successful leadership style: “I taught my team a long time ago what we call the ‘but for’ test. But for you taking this action or that action, this change or the result would not have happened. If others are already doing it, then focus on something else.”
Regarding his remaining months in office, DeWine said, “I don’t spend much time thinking about legacy. Instead, I intend to help all Ohioans reach their full God-given potential.”
Summarizing her boss, chief advisor O’Donnell said, “He is the real deal, one of the last of a rare breed of public servants.”
Myra Adams served on the creative team of two Republican presidential campaigns in 2004 and 2008. Read more from her archive at The Hill.

articles.title: Democratic momentum keeps rolling in race for Senate
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Dems’ chances rise in key Senate races ▪ Bond market remains unsettled ▪ Trump campaigning for Darline Graham ▪ Stars and Stripes in the Pentagon’s crosshairs Democrats are riding a wave of momentum as they look to expand their Senate map, with new forecasts offering fresh optimism that flipping the upper…
articles.body:
▪ Dems’ chances rise in key Senate races

▪ Stars and Stripes in the Pentagon’s crosshairs

Democrats are riding a wave of momentum as they look to expand their Senate map, with new forecasts offering fresh optimism that flipping the upper chamber could be within reach.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report on Thursday shifted the Senate races in Texas and Iowa toward Democrats, rating both as “toss-ups.” Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) similarly rates them as toss-ups.

“Even though, on paper, it should be extraordinarily difficult for Democrats to flip seats that Trump won by more than 13 points, it’s increasingly hard to ignore both public and private polling showing them to be more competitive than the Lean category reflects,” Jessica Taylor , Cook Political Report’s Senate and governors editor, wrote in an analysis.

Texas Democratic Senate nominee, state Rep. James Talarico , has consistently polled even better than Beto O’Rourke did in 2018 — the closest Democrats have recently come to winning a Senate seat in the state. Talarico’s favorability ratings remain net positive, as his scandal-prone GOP opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton , remains underwater by double digits.

In Iowa, Rep. Ashley Hinson (R) is a formidable candidate, but the tough political environment has hit Iowa especially hard , as the agriculture-dependent economy contends with President Trump ’s tariffs, along with the rising prices for fertilizer and diesel due to the Iran war.

She faces Josh Turek , a two-time Paralympic gold medalist in wheelchair basketball who represents a state House district that Trump won by 9 points in 2024.

Democrats also got some encouraging results in Alaska on Tuesday, when former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) got 48 percent of the primary vote and incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) received nearly 43 percent of the vote. With no other serious contenders in the all-party primary, it served as something of a dress rehearsal before they face off again in November.

Democrats need to net four seats to win the majority in the Senate, a hefty undertaking in an election year with a map that structurally favors Republicans. But the downstream impact of Trump’s sinking approval rating, along with historic headwinds facing the majority party, has started to open up seats that once looked like long shots.

Trump won Ohio by more than 11 points in 2024 — the largest presidential margin of victory the state had seen in 40 years — but the Senate race is now considered a toss-up, as incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R) vies to serve the rest of Vice President Vance ’s Senate term after being appointed last year to the seat.

He faces a strong opponent in former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D), who narrowly lost his reelection bid to Sen. Bernie Moreno (R) in 2024. The Hill’s Helen Huiskes reports that the backlash to data centers could be a decisive factor if Husted goes down.

Kansas is also seen as a long-shot chance for Democrats to grab a seat, with megachurch Rev. Adam Hamilton , the Democratic nominee, holding a significant fundraising advantage over incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R). Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted its rating of the race from safe to likely Republican earlier this month after Hamilton won the nomination.

Moderate Republican Sen. Susan Collins has been able to hold on for years in the blue-leaning Maine, but Democrats are newly energized after replacing Graham Platner with Troy Jackson on their ticket.

Republicans are bullish on their chances of slipping the open Senate seat in Michigan, where former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers is facing progressive former health official Abdul El-Sayed .

A loss for Democrats in Michigan or Maine could put flipping the Senate out of reach. While Republicans have a financial advantage, Democrats have the clear edge when it comes to voter enthusiasm, DDHQ chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley said in an interview.

Democrats also lead in the generic congressional ballot, with 46 percent of Americans saying they’d back the average Democrat, compared to 40 percent who would back the average Republican, if the election were held today, according to DDHQ’s aggregator.

The national political landscape has become increasingly important as politics becomes less local, said Skelley. According to the latest polling average, 38 percent of voters approve of the job Trump is doing, down 2 points from last week and 4 points from last month.

“The fundamental problems for the president’s party have not changed. In fact, some of them have worsened,” Skelley said, pointing to gas prices and the ongoing Iran crisis.

“Basically, every time that seems to heat up… Democrats’ lead on the generic ballot grows a little bit, and President Trump’s approval rating sinks a little bit more.”

DDHQ puts Republicans’ chances of winning the Senate at 54 percent and Democrats’ at 46 percent, a significant narrowing of the GOP’s 20-point advantage over Democrats last month.

“For practical purposes, it’s a coin flip,” Skelley said, “which, I think, if you told Democrats six months ago, a year ago, that they had roughly a coin flip’s chance of winning the Senate, they would have been like, ‘Well, that’s great.’ Because it didn’t look that way a year ago.”

▪ The Hill : Cook Political Report moves Texas, Iowa governor’s races toward Dems.

▪ The Hill : El-Sayed holds slight lead in Michigan in AARP poll.

The list is now growing by the day of candidates on the November ballot calling for tougher regulations on data center buildouts, with Rogers, the Michigan GOP nominee, the latest on Thursday. Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) represents parts of northern Virginia, which has the greatest number of data centers nationwide. He offered a warning when I spoke with him Thursday night.

“ People talk about the issue with China, but honestly, the people who are seeing their utility bills double and triple don’t care about the race against China. We’re going to lose that race because 70 percent of Americans now don’t want data centers in their community,” Subramanyam told me.

This is part of the balance that lawmakers are going to have to deal with in the coming years: listening to the concerns of their constituents, while also weighing the national security concerns of potentially losing ground to China in the AI battle.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

Trump took part in a discussion with his former fixer Michael Cohen on Thursday, suggesting the lawyer was “forced” to testify against the president during his 2024 hush money trial in New York. The full conversation, which marks a full circle moment in the pair’s apparent reconciliation, will air on Sunday.

The Democratic National Committee has narrowed down the list of possible cities for its 2028 convention to three — Philadelphia, Boston and Denver. The location is expected to be finalized in the coming months.

House Democrats are calling on Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to abandon plans to equip immigration agents with electric shock gloves, The Hill’s Rebecca Beitsch exclusively reports . The Democrats on the Homeland Security panel argued it requires significant training and restraint on officers’ part, placing the public at risk.

FILE – The Treasury Department building is pictured at dusk in Washington, June 6, 2019. (AP Photo/Patrick Semansky, File)

SHAKY GROUND : The bond market doesn’t appear to be settling down, at least so far, despite the moves from the Trump administration to try to quell concerns.

The 30-year Treasury bond yield stood at 5.25 percent as of the end of the day Thursday, just below the 5.3 percent mark it reached on Tuesday, the highest yield since April 2007. That was just months before the start of a financial crisis that became the Great Recession and upended the global economy.

The yield on the 30-year bond hasn’t closed at under 5 percent since July 6.

The Treasury Department announced Wednesday it would double the maximum amount of the country’s long-term debt that it can buy back starting on Sept. 9 and lasting through at least Nov. 4. And Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he is willing to intervene further during an interview with CNBC on Thursday.

Experts told The Hill’s Julia Manchester and Max Rego that unpredictability surrounding the Iran war, the president’s tariff policies, increased spending on AI and the soaring national debt are contributing to the volatile economic situation.

Markets did initially rally in response to the Treasury Department’s move, sending bond yields down and the price of gold and silver up. But the yield rose again on Thursday.

▪ The Hill : What to know about the bond market situation.

▪ The Associated Press : Why the Treasury’s moves haven’t worked so far.

▪ Reuters : Federal Reserve officials tread carefully.

HITTING THE HOMESTRETCH : Trump will travel to South Carolina today to make a pitch trying to help Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) get across the finish line ahead of her Senate primary runoff next week.

Graham is seeking the Republican nomination for a full six-year term in place of her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), but must fend off a challenge from Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.).

The president has endorsed Graham, the sibling of his onetime-adversary-turned-ally, but Norman may have an opening after Graham’s lack of experience was on display at their debate earlier this week.

Graham was asked a question about whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are U.S. national security issues, and she responded that she’s “not that informed on national security.”

Graham defended her comments by saying that she’s not a “career politician.” But the incident speaks directly to the attacks she’s received from critics who say she is too inexperienced to serve a full term.

▪ The Hill : Trump seeks to boost Graham ahead of runoff.

▪ The State : Will top South Carolina Republicans endorse in the race?

CLOSING IN : A top Canadian official signaled that Canada and the U.S. are close to finalizing a deal to avoid Trump’s threatened tariffs as the latest deadline approaches.

Unless Trump issues an extension or a deal is reached, 50 percent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods are set to take effect at midnight. Trump delayed the implementation of the tariffs for three days on Tuesday as he said the two countries were approaching a deal.

Dominic LeBlanc , the minister for Canada-U.S. trade, was in Washington, D.C., again on Thursday to meet with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer for talks.

“We’re very close. We continue to make progress,” LeBlanc said.

The terms of the deal have yet to be released.

▪ The Associated Press : Canadian premier says Trump is a ‘bad person.’

FREEZE : GOP Sen. Kevin Cramer (N.D.) said he’s placing a hold on all Trump nominees in protest of the administration’s wetlands policy.

Cramer told The Hill in a statement that he’s disappointed the administration is leaving a Biden-era rule on wetlands in place for now, leading to his decision to block Trump nominees. E&E News first reported Cramer’s position.

“My farmers are furious and so am I. There won’t be another nominee confirmed until something changes,” he said, calling the rule favored by “environmental extremists.”

The rule seeks to prevent the draining of wetlands protected under conservation easements, protecting duck habitats.

Holds can slow the process of confirming nominees in the Senate, requiring the chamber to spend hours debating them and taking additional votes.

▪ The Hill : Trump lifts summer gas restrictions early.

PROPERTY SEARCH : The FBI reportedly carried out a search of former Rep. Eric Swalwell ’s (D-Calif.) home on Sunday as part of an investigation into sexual assault allegations against him.

Sources familiar with the investigation told CNN that federal agents seized electronic devices from Swalwell at the San Francisco airport a day before the raid at his home. Four women confirmed to the outlet that they have been contacted by the FBI as part of a federal investigation into the former congressman.

Swalwell was the front-runner in the California gubernatorial race when multiple allegations of sexual misconduct came out against him. He denies wrongdoing, but the controversy led him to drop out of the race and resign from office.

A special election to replace Swalwell in the House was held on Tuesday. DDHQ projected Thursday that California state Sen. Aisha Wahab (D) will win the seat to serve the remainder of Swalwell’s term.

▪ Los Angeles Times : Swalwell briefly detained, source says.

The president will participate in photo opportunities at 11 a.m. He will travel to Myrtle Beach, S.C., to deliver remarks at 7 p.m. and return to the White House after.

The Pentagon is seen from the air, July 15, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon, File)

STARS AND STRIPES : The battle over the editorial independence of the military news outlet Stars and Stripes has moved into the spotlight following the retirement announcement from the paper’s longtime publisher.

A trio of Senate Democrats sent a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday to defend the outlet’s independence. Publisher Max Lederer , who has led the paper as publisher since 2007, announced Tuesday that he would retire at the end of next month amid issues over the Pentagon’s attempts to direct coverage.

He said his philosophy of leadership and “understanding of the value and mission” of the outlet is different in “fundamental ways” from the plans that the Pentagon has for it.

The announcement came after the Defense Department appointed an active-duty Navy captain, William Urban , to be the publisher’s deputy without consulting Lederer.

Democratic Sens. Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Elizabeth Warren (Mass.) and Jeanne Shaheen (N.H.) said in the letter that the appointment of Urban “raises serious questions” about the paper’s independence.

The Pentagon has sought to mold Stars and Stripes’s editorial output during Trump’s second term, outlining changes in an eight-page memo released in March. The memo included a requirement that content be “consistent with good order and discipline of the military.”

Top Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in January that the department would “refocus” the outlet away from “woke distractions that syphon morale.”

Stars and Stripes has operated independently from the Pentagon under a framework established in 1994, even though its staff are department employees and the outlet receives partial funding from the agency.

▪ CBS News : Pentagon considers firing publisher ahead of retirement.

▪ The Hill : Army plans to phase out drone unit championed by sacked generals.

President Trump, right, meets with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on Sentosa Island in Singapore, on June 12, 2018.

REKINDLING THE SPARK : Trump is pushing to resume his bromance with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un , The Hill’s Mallory Wilson reports , but experts are cautioning that doing so is likely to be fruitless and could harm the U.S. alliance with South Korea.

Trump this week told reporters he plans to meet with Kim later this year but did not provide additional details about when a meeting could take place. The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump has privately discussed setting up an in-person discussion with the North Korean leader when he’s next in Asia, which would likely be in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation in China.

“The fact that I get along with him — that’s a good thing, not a bad thing,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday. “He has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons. Should have never allowed it to happen. If I was president, I wouldn’t have allowed it to happen. But he’s got them.”

Trump met with Kim three times during his first term, but denuclearization talks stalled, and Kim showed no interest in diplomacy under the Biden administration.

On Sunday, Trump announced that he was ordering the Pentagon to reduce the U.S.’s participation in joint military exercises with South Korea this week, in part to avoid irking Kim.

Michael Sobolik , a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, told Wilson that scaling down military exercises with South Korea worked during Trump’s first term to secure a meeting with Kim, but he was skeptical the same tactic would work this time around.

“It’s pretty clear from the first term that he views America’s relationship with South Korea as a complicating factor in his ability to negotiate directly with Kim,” Sobolik said. “The main question I’m asking right now is: What’s Kim’s price going to be for face-to-face meetings with Trump?”

▪ Reuters : China blames U.S. for Korea tensions.

▪ BBC : Trump wants to be friends with Kim, but South Korea could pay the price.

Could Iran try a midterms October surprise? Marc A. Thiessen writes in The Hill.

Americans are getting caught in the safety net , former House Speaker Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) and Les Ford write in The Wall Street Journal.

The U.S. Capitol is seen beyond the Freedom 250 Grand Prix race track, Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

And finally … 👏👏👏 Congrats to this week’s Morning Report quiz winners ! They were revved up for this racing quiz.

Here’s who went 4/4: Richard Baznik, Jess Elger, Stan Wasser, Chuck Schoenenberger, Ned Sauthoff, Harry Strulovici, Rick Schmidtke, Vicenta Montoya, Linda L. Field, Lou Tisler, Bob Hickerson, Mark R. Williamson, Carmine Petracca, Pam Manges and Steve James .

West Palm Beach is the city that is not on the list of this year’s locations for the IndyCar series.

The race was extended from 125 laps to 147 because that produces a 250-mile racetrack .

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum worked along with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to design the course. Despite having many jobs, this was not one of them for Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The National Gallery of Art conducted a study on the impact of the expected high speeds on its artwork. The gallery declined to release specifics of the study but implemented safety measures for its staff, visitors, collections and facilities.

Michael Sobolik , a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, told Wilson that scaling down military exercises with South Korea worked during Trump’s first term to secure a meeting with Kim, but he was skeptical the same tactic would work this time around.

“It’s pretty clear from the first term that he views America’s relationship with South Korea as a complicating factor in his ability to negotiate directly with Kim,” Sobolik said. “The main question I’m asking right now is: What’s Kim’s price going to be for face-to-face meetings with Trump?”

articles.title: 8 killed in plane crash at remote Alaska radar site: US military
articles.summary: Eight people were killed after the charter airplane they were traveling on crashed in Alaska on Thursday afternoon, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The crash occurred near the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, a U.S. Air Force military airstrip located in a remote area in the southwest part of the state.…
articles.body:
Eight people were killed after the charter airplane they were traveling on crashed in Alaska on Thursday afternoon, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

The crash occurred near the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, a U.S. Air Force military airstrip located in a remote area in the southwest part of the state.

U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert Davis called the fatal crash a “devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve” in a statement reported by The Associated Press .

The crash occurred around noon local time on Thursday, after the aircraft departed Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport en route to Cape Newenham, according to a preliminary FAA report.

The agency said it will work jointly with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) on an investigation into the crash.

An NTSB spokesperson told The Hill on Friday morning that five of its investigators are traveling to the site of the crash to document the scene.

The NTSB investigators will examine flight tracking data, air traffic control communications, weather forecasts, aircraft maintenance records, witness statements and other information, according to the board spokesperson.

Alaska Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R) and Dan Sullivan (R) extended their thoughts and prayers following the news of the crash.

“I join Alaskans in condolences as we learn of the plane crash in Cape Newenham today,” Murkowski wrote on the social platform X .

“I’ve traveled extensively with Security Aviation throughout Alaska, and have met many of their experienced pilots,” the senator continued. “I appreciate the U.S. Coast Guard, NTSB, Alaska State Troopers, and the Rescue Coordination Center for responding to the site.”

She added, “Alaska is praying for those on board, their loved ones, and the team at Security Aviation.”

Sullivan similarly expressed his condolences to the people who lost loved ones in the crash and said he will seek updates from the joint investigation.

“Julie and I join our fellow Alaskans in praying for the families and loved ones of those who were killed today in a plane crash in Western Alaska,” he wrote online. “I’ve asked for a briefing from the NTSB and the FAA as we all seek answers on what caused this horrific tragedy.”

articles.title: Polls can mislead: Do your own homework before you vote
articles.summary: After big misses from several polls in recent weeks, people are wondering what to believe.
articles.body:
Headlines recently touted a new Siena Research Institute poll claiming that Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York City, enjoys an approval rating of 69 percent .

I don’t believe that. Conversations that I have had with bodega owners, taxi drivers, construction workers and people in many other occupations lead to a different conclusion. New Yorkers cannot stand our smug young socialist mayor.

Am I not talking to the right people? Do such surveys reliably reflect the mood of the electorate?

After big misses from several polls in recent weeks, people are wondering what to believe. Of course, survey failures are nothing new; President Trump has consistently outperformed his polling, causing many supporters to view the entire industry as suspect.

For sure, polling can influence voters. If your candidate is crashing in the polls ahead of an election, you may decide it’s not worth voting — that the outcome is preordained and your vote won’t matter. Or, you may decide against donating to a campaign, not wanting to waste your money.

Remember that one month after his 2024 win, then President-elect Trump sued the Des Moines Register and its former pollster, J. Ann Selzer, for “brazen election interference” over a poll published just days before the election.

Selzer’s Nov. 2 survey showed Democrat Kamala Harris winning reliably red Iowa by 3 to 4 points — a shocking outlier that received a lot of attention at a critical moment in the campaign. Just days later, Trump won Iowa by 13 points . Although Trump later dropped his lawsuit, many agreed that Selzer’s survey had been intended to shake his supporters’ confidence in a race he was quite clearly winning. She quit her job soon thereafter.

Since that 2024 race, the rise of prediction and betting platforms has upped the stakes. People placing bets on political races will have even greater incentives to try to influence or manipulate polling. The smaller the race, the more vulnerable the poll.

Not all polls are trustworthy. Siena is generally deemed accurate, with one group rating it as having a “ slight Democratic lean. ” But sometimes, even an honest poll can produce a misleading result, as with the Siena poll that had Mamdani fans cheering.

The institute set out to assess the current state of the governor’s race in New York, and surveyed 811 “likely New York gubernatorial voters.” As such, they included only 227 people in New York City . But that figure is meaningless, as it represents less than .003 percent of the 8.8 million people living in the Big Apple. Of that tiny group, 69 percent approved of the mayor, while only 49 percent gave a thumbs-up to the Democratic Socialists of America, Mamdani’s political home base. That inconsistency typifies the screwy results that come with small samples. If New Yorkers like the mayor, shouldn’t they also like his platform?

Steve Greenberg, who works for the Siena Research Institute, told me that the poll’s samples were starkly different from what Siena might have included if they had aimed to determine Mamdani’s actual popularity.

Because the poll focused on the governor’s race, the survey overweighted areas outside the city. In those regions, the mayor fared poorly, registering approval of only 34 percent in the suburbs and 41 percent upstate. Also, non-white voters were undercounted; some 71 percent of respondents were white , whereas only 10 percent were Black and 13 percent Latino. Also unusual is that of those surveyed, more than half reportedly had incomes above $100,000, whereas the median income in New York State is just shy of $86,000 .

Bottom line: because it set out to measure trends in the New York state governor’s race, the Siena poll ended up inadvertently favoring Mamdani, overrepresenting whites with high incomes. The questionable accuracy of the reading, of course, did not preclude Mamdani supporters from jumping on the poll, to tout his supposed popularity.

Other polls — some big misses — have also recently raised eyebrows. In the run-up to the Democratic primary for an open Senate seat in Michigan, polling showed far-left candidate Abdul El-Sayed running away with the contest, up by double digits over establishment favorite Haley Stevens. On primary night, El-Sayed won by only 1 point. Some theorize that the polling has distorted the popularity of Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates because white liberals are more likely to respond to polls than other Democrats.

But on the same night, in another Democratic Senate primary, progressive Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) beat out Rep. Angie Craig (D) by nearly 20 percentage points , despite some surveys showing a neck-and-neck contest .

And then there was an actual polling scandal. Median Strategies, a group describing itself as an “independent research and polling” organization on a website that has subsequently disappeared , confessed to creating completely bogus polls . One showed Francesca Hong, a socialist candidate who ran in the Democratic primary for Wisconsin governor, some 20 or more points ahead of rival Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley. Crowley, a moderate, ended up winning. Another poll from Median put incumbent Karen Bass ahead of opponent Nithya Raman in the Los Angeles mayoral contest by almost 12 points.

Median claimed on its now defunct website that it “ fabricated the polls as part of a ‘short-term social experiment'” meant to show “how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification,” as reported by The New York Times. Since Bass posted the poll on X, it spread far and wide, boosting her numbers.

Who was behind that deception and why they did it remain to be seen. But the message is clear: Do not accept polling at face value. Look at the cross-tabs to see who was counted, who performed the survey and, most important — pick a candidate whose policies and personality appear best suited for the job.

The most important takeaway is this: do your own research and don’t go with the crowd, because sometimes we have no idea where the crowd is actually headed.

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

articles.title: Whole Hog Politics: A chilly forecast for the Senate GOP from Alaska
articles.summary: [Watch Whole Hog Politics live: Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. EDT as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon break down this week’s political news and answer questions from a live online audience.] Elon Musk may succeed in November at repealing Alaska’s nonpartisan primary system. Whether you think that’s a…
articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. EDT as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon break down this week’s political news and answer questions from a live online audience. ] Elon Musk may succeed in November at repealing Alaska’s nonpartisan primary system. Whether you think that’s a good thing or not probably depends on whether you’re a Republican who wants to stop worrying about a state that for decades was more reliably red than parts of the Deep South.

But if you’re an election forecaster, you will miss Alaska’s system if Musk and Co. succeed. With one of the latest primaries on the calendar, Alaska gives us an invaluable look at where voters are heading in a general election now just 74 days away.

As of this writing, with perhaps as much as 20 percent of the vote presumably still drifting in on malamute dogsleds or carried like abalone in the paws of adorable sea otters, former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is the top vote-getter in Alaska’s nonpartisan primary, leading incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by more than 5 points.

But if you add up all the Republican candidates in the field ( including the other Dan Sullivan ), 48 percent of the vote went to Republican candidates — almost 2 points more than Peltola’s current share. But she wasn’t the only Democrat running, either. Add in the Democratic also-rans, and the blue share of the electorate clocks in at 50 percent.

This is hardly to say that this means that Peltola will win in November by 2 points, but this is an awfully good indication of how the electorate is looking with the general election very nearly upon us. Good polling, as we have often observed and has been proven quite right of late , is very hard to come by these days. But in a nonpartisan primary, you get a live feed on how persuadable voters are breaking.

This is the third cycle in which Alaska has had its everyone-in-the-pool primary in effect, and in contested statewide races, most notably the 2022 gubernatorial race , primary results have been strongly predictive of the general. And with Peltola proving herself to be a savvy campaigner with moves like saying thanks, but no thanks to an unsolicited endorsement from former Vice President Kamala Harris, Peltola definitely looks like she’s in the driver’s seat. We’ll check back on the final margins, though, after all the malamutes and otters bring in the last ballots.

[ Programming alert: Watch “The Hill Sunday” with Chris Stirewalt – Get the latest from decisionmakers from around the country and Washington insiders. And, as always, we’ll get expert analysis from our best-in-the-business panel of journalists, including Julie Mason of SiriusXM and Ian Swanson of The Hill. Be sure to catch us on NewsNation at 10 a.m. EDT / 9 a.m. CDT or your local CW station.]
