The Wall Street Journal : “Eight colorful prints by modern master Henri Matisse that were stolen last year from a Brazilian library during an armed daytime heist have been recovered and safely returned, São Paulo police said. The Matisse works, which police valued at roughly $190,000, came from the artist’s famed 1947 ‘Jazz’ print series and featured images of a clown and a cowboy, among other imagery. Police recovered the prints last week when they raided an apartment in the São Paulo suburb of São Bernardo do Campo and arrested a man suspected of watching over the stolen art. … The brazenness of the theft rattled art circles. Two armed thieves stormed the marble-floored Mário de Andrade public library in broad daylight, just after 10 a.m. on Dec. 7. They lifted their shirts to show the security guard they had guns and threatened an elderly couple nearby before stealing the art off the library’s walls and escaping on foot minutes later. Police said they feared the Portinari works may have already been resold on the black market. The Matisses were returned to the library last Thursday.”

Dems take populist pitchforks to data centers: Semafor : “As populist pushback builds against the AI industry and data centers that power it, Republicans who have cheered the AI boom are scrambling to find a new identity as middle-ground pragmatists. Instead of a moratorium on building new facilities, a growing number of GOP candidates have called for ‘guardrails’ to protect skeptical communities from unchecked AI growth, as well as the rollback of industry tax breaks. These Republicans’ rebrand also involves a bid for the high ground by attacking Democrats with more nuanced positions on data centers. They’re aligned with President Donald Trump ’s White House, which tried to blunt anti-AI activists’ momentum with a voluntary ‘ratepayer protection pledge,’ released in March with industry promises to foot the bill for the power demand from new data centers. Data centers “could use a little public relations help,’ Trump said on Wednesday.”

GOP Senate campaign arm tells AI industry to pony up: Axios : “The Senate GOP campaign arm, in a private memo to top AI companies, warns that toxic views of U.S. data centers are killing the party’s chances of holding a vital seat in Ohio. In the memo, obtained by Axios, the National Republican Senatorial Committee says Democrats have made data centers a ‘centerpiece’ of their campaign to defeat Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) — and that it’s working. ‘If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one,’ the memo says. ‘This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.’ Republicans want the AI companies to do whatever it takes to stem the public backlash. AI CEOs and top Republicans share in the rising panic. They tell us internal polls show data centers are as popular as spent nuclear waste, and more broadly have become a proxy for feelings about AI. Tech giants are scrambling to pull together media campaigns to try to shift opinion before it hardens locally and nationally. But Democrats aren’t dummies. They see the same polls and are moving fast.”

A rural revolt in Texas: Politico : “Rural voters may not stop the spread of data centers, but they could stop Texas Gov. Greg Abbott. The Republican is bleeding support from small towns as he seeks a fourth term because of two late-emerging issues: power-hungry tech campuses and a planned $33 billion electric transmission build-out. Pushback against Abbott points to larger fears about losing rural identities, but also to everyday concerns about construction, pollution and tight supplies of water and electricity. Shawn Nanny, a Republican county commissioner in West Texas, said data centers and power line plans are the ‘straws that broke the camel’s back’ when it comes to Abbott and other Texas GOP leaders. Some longtime conservatives are now considering the unthinkable — voting in November for a Democrat to be Texas’ next governor. And Abbott’s August directive to pause Texas data center grid approvals hasn’t convinced all of them to vote for him.”

Talarico opens door to Cornyn voters with high-profile hire: The Hill : “Texas state Sen. James Talarico ’s (D) campaign team on Monday confirmed it poached a former staffer for Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) to join him on the campaign trail months ahead of the midterm elections. Jacob Smith , who served as deputy legislative director for Cornyn, will now serve as deputy policy director for the Democratic senatorial campaign in the Lone Star State. ‘I’ve worked for Republicans like Senator Cornyn my entire career, but this year I’m proud to be joining James Talarico’s campaign. Instead of playing partisan politics, Talarico speaks to the needs of everyday people who day in and day out work too hard for too little,’ Smith said in a statement to The Hill.”

Ossoff trolls Trump over female aide and reaps results: The New York Times : “She never takes a day off, not even on Sunday. She works out of the Oval Office and she’s got a regular seat on Marine One. She texts with world leaders on the president’s behalf. She stays up late with him drafting social media posts. She rarely speaks on camera and yet she is never not there, ever-present with a wide smile and her eyes fixed on the president. She is Natalie Harp , the 35-year-old West Wing aide who is the utmost gatekeeper to President Trump, a one-woman conduit of information operating entirely outside the usual chain of command. The public’s interest in Ms. Harp exploded after she was revealed last week to be one of the lucky few who joined the president inside an airplane catering container to be whisked out of Turkey under threat of attack by Iran. This week she became the subject of a political attack line delivered by Jon Ossoff , the Democratic senator from Georgia, who said of the president: ‘He doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar.’”

Pity the body men and body women: NOTUS : “There’s a secretive cadre of young staffers whose job it is to make the Senate run more efficiently. They’re known informally as the ‘Body Guy Caucus,’ though some are women. They can be found by most senators’ sides, helping them navigate the maze of hallways, tunnels and subways in the Capitol complex as well as the crowds of reporters outside the Senate chamber who are eager to pounce on their bosses for a quote. While most congressional staffers tend to work out of an office, a body person spends nearly every waking hour shadowing their boss, performing a unique set of duties that include valet, scheduler, traffic cop and sometimes even emotional support animal. It’s a position of trust many senators take very seriously, and one that comes with a high level of stress. ‘It is the craziest position to have on the Hill, and it is the best position to have on the Hill, because you have these 22-year-olds that are more or less babysitting some of the most important and powerful people in the country,’ one former body person told NOTUS.”

Is Darline Graham’s gaffe sufficient to give Norman a chance on Tuesday?: The Hill : “Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Wednesday defended her stumble earlier this week on a national security question during a primary runoff debate, saying she was simply being ‘honest’ about her lack of political experience. ‘I tripped up on one question last night regarding Taiwan,’ Graham said in an interview with Fox News on Wednesday. ‘I have said many times I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician.’ Graham, who was appointed to fill the vacancy left after her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), died last month, was asked during the special GOP debate on Tuesday whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the U.S. and why. ‘I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security,’ she responded. ‘But I do support the military.’”

Dems ready to write off Florida Senate race after DSA upset: Politico: “Progressive Angie Nixon ’s stunning upset in Florida’s Senate race has many Democrats in the state spiraling. The Jacksonville lawmaker’s primary victory on Tuesday night over retired Lt. Col. Alexander Vindman jolted a state few thought would hold any surprises. But it also rattled Democrats who worry about her chances against GOP Sen. Ashley Moody in a state that hasn’t picked a Democrat for Senate since 2012. They’re concerned about Nixon’s ability to team up with other candidates and fundraise for down-ballot hopefuls — as Vindman appeared poised to do with his “resistance movement,” Trump-impeachment-era fundraising network. They’re also worried about her more contentious positions, including her decision to join the Democratic Socialists of America in June, in a state where Republicans have 1.5 million more registered voters than Democrats.”

New Mexico’s Democratic governor soaking up the attention from 2028 field — Politico

The pollster Median Strategies was fabricating their data … for fun — The New York Times

Extended naval deployments and the president’s stated indifference costing GOP in Norfolk-based House race — The Washington Post

Abdul El-Sayed leads in new Michigan Senate poll by 7 points — The Hill

Missouri gerrymandering is approved for midterms by a Circuit Court judge — The New York Times

Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) spotted snooping in constituent’s mailbox — TMZ

“This is a non-story” — White House spokesperson Olivia Wales, when asked why President Trump claims that mail-in voting is “inherently corrupt,” yet voted by mail Tuesday.

“Hey, why’d you put it in that order?” — Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) when asked about a potential Ossoff and Kelly presidential ticket.

“Since you mentioned crucial Waukesha County, I couldn’t resist offering up this delicious nugget from Tuesday’s results (if you’re a Democrat, at least). I went back to 2018’s primary, which had similar partisan dynamics. Democrats blew the doors off the place, doubling their votes in the county. Tom Tiffany got 6,000 fewer votes. Turnout was about equal between the parties. And the most WOW [Waukesha, Ozaukee and Washington counties] part of WOW? Francesca Hong got 5,000 more votes than Tony Evers . In Waukesha! Can you even believe it! Maybe crucial Waukesha isn’t quite the slayer of Democratic dreams it used to be.” — Mark Kliesen, Atlanta

paragraphs: [ Watch Whole Hog Politics live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. EDT as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon break down this week’s political news and answer questions from a live online audience. ] Elon Musk may succeed in November at repealing Alaska’s nonpartisan primary system. Whether you think that’s a good thing or not probably depends on whether you’re a Republican who wants to stop worrying about a state that for decades was more reliably red than parts of the Deep South.

But if you’re an election forecaster, you will miss Alaska’s system if Musk and Co. succeed. With one of the latest primaries on the calendar, Alaska gives us an invaluable look at where voters are heading in a general election now just 74 days away.

As of this writing, with perhaps as much as 20 percent of the vote presumably still drifting in on malamute dogsleds or carried like abalone in the paws of adorable sea otters, former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is the top vote-getter in Alaska’s nonpartisan primary, leading incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by more than 5 points.

But if you add up all the Republican candidates in the field ( including the other Dan Sullivan ), 48 percent of the vote went to Republican candidates — almost 2 points more than Peltola’s current share. But she wasn’t the only Democrat running, either. Add in the Democratic also-rans, and the blue share of the electorate clocks in at 50 percent.

This is hardly to say that this means that Peltola will win in November by 2 points, but this is an awfully good indication of how the electorate is looking with the general election very nearly upon us. Good polling, as we have often observed and has been proven quite right of late , is very hard to come by these days. But in a nonpartisan primary, you get a live feed on how persuadable voters are breaking.

This is the third cycle in which Alaska has had its everyone-in-the-pool primary in effect, and in contested statewide races, most notably the 2022 gubernatorial race , primary results have been strongly predictive of the general. And with Peltola proving herself to be a savvy campaigner with moves like saying thanks, but no thanks to an unsolicited endorsement from former Vice President Kamala Harris, Peltola definitely looks like she’s in the driver’s seat. We’ll check back on the final margins, though, after all the malamutes and otters bring in the last ballots.

The Wall Street Journal : “Eight colorful prints by modern master Henri Matisse that were stolen last year from a Brazilian library during an armed daytime heist have been recovered and safely returned, São Paulo police said. The Matisse works, which police valued at roughly $190,000, came from the artist’s famed 1947 ‘Jazz’ print series and featured images of a clown and a cowboy, among other imagery. Police recovered the prints last week when they raided an apartment in the São Paulo suburb of São Bernardo do Campo and arrested a man suspected of watching over the stolen art. … The brazenness of the theft rattled art circles. Two armed thieves stormed the marble-floored Mário de Andrade public library in broad daylight, just after 10 a.m. on Dec. 7. They lifted their shirts to show the security guard they had guns and threatened an elderly couple nearby before stealing the art off the library’s walls and escaping on foot minutes later. Police said they feared the Portinari works may have already been resold on the black market. The Matisses were returned to the library last Thursday.”

Instead of a moratorium on building new facilities, a growing number of GOP candidates have called for ‘guardrails’ to protect skeptical communities from unchecked AI growth, as well as the rollback of industry tax breaks. These Republicans’ rebrand also involves a bid for the high ground by attacking Democrats with more nuanced positions on data centers. They’re aligned with President Donald Trump ’s White House, which tried to blunt anti-AI activists’ momentum with a voluntary ‘ratepayer protection pledge,’ released in March with industry promises to foot the bill for the power demand from new data centers. Data centers “could use a little public relations help,’ Trump said on Wednesday.”

In the memo, obtained by Axios, the National Republican Senatorial Committee says Democrats have made data centers a ‘centerpiece’ of their campaign to defeat Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) — and that it’s working. ‘If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one,’ the memo says. ‘This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.’ Republicans want the AI companies to do whatever it takes to stem the public backlash. AI CEOs and top Republicans share in the rising panic. They tell us internal polls show data centers are as popular as spent nuclear waste, and more broadly have become a proxy for feelings about AI. Tech giants are scrambling to pull together media campaigns to try to shift opinion before it hardens locally and nationally. But Democrats aren’t dummies. They see the same polls and are moving fast.”

The Republican is bleeding support from small towns as he seeks a fourth term because of two late-emerging issues: power-hungry tech campuses and a planned $33 billion electric transmission build-out. Pushback against Abbott points to larger fears about losing rural identities, but also to everyday concerns about construction, pollution and tight supplies of water and electricity. Shawn Nanny, a Republican county commissioner in West Texas, said data centers and power line plans are the ‘straws that broke the camel’s back’ when it comes to Abbott and other Texas GOP leaders. Some longtime conservatives are now considering the unthinkable — voting in November for a Democrat to be Texas’ next governor. And Abbott’s August directive to pause Texas data center grid approvals hasn’t convinced all of them to vote for him.”

Talarico opens door to Cornyn voters with high-profile hire: The Hill : “Texas state Sen. James Talarico ’s (D) campaign team on Monday confirmed it poached a former staffer for Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) to join him on the campaign trail months ahead of the midterm elections. Jacob Smith , who served as deputy legislative director for Cornyn, will now serve as deputy policy director for the Democratic senatorial campaign in the Lone Star State. ‘I’ve worked for Republicans like Senator Cornyn my entire career, but this year I’m proud to be joining James Talarico’s campaign. Instead of playing partisan politics, Talarico speaks to the needs of everyday people who day in and day out work too hard for too little,’ Smith said in a statement to The Hill.”

Ossoff trolls Trump over female aide and reaps results: The New York Times : “She never takes a day off, not even on Sunday. She works out of the Oval Office and she’s got a regular seat on Marine One. She texts with world leaders on the president’s behalf. She stays up late with him drafting social media posts. She rarely speaks on camera and yet she is never not there, ever-present with a wide smile and her eyes fixed on the president. She is Natalie Harp , the 35-year-old West Wing aide who is the utmost gatekeeper to President Trump, a one-woman conduit of information operating entirely outside the usual chain of command. The public’s interest in Ms. Harp exploded after she was revealed last week to be one of the lucky few who joined the president inside an airplane catering container to be whisked out of Turkey under threat of attack by Iran. This week she became the subject of a political attack line delivered by Jon Ossoff , the Democratic senator from Georgia, who said of the president: ‘He doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar.’”

Pity the body men and body women: NOTUS : “There’s a secretive cadre of young staffers whose job it is to make the Senate run more efficiently. They’re known informally as the ‘Body Guy Caucus,’ though some are women. They can be found by most senators’ sides, helping them navigate the maze of hallways, tunnels and subways in the Capitol complex as well as the crowds of reporters outside the Senate chamber who are eager to pounce on their bosses for a quote. While most congressional staffers tend to work out of an office, a body person spends nearly every waking hour shadowing their boss, performing a unique set of duties that include valet, scheduler, traffic cop and sometimes even emotional support animal. It’s a position of trust many senators take very seriously, and one that comes with a high level of stress. ‘It is the craziest position to have on the Hill, and it is the best position to have on the Hill, because you have these 22-year-olds that are more or less babysitting some of the most important and powerful people in the country,’ one former body person told NOTUS.”

Is Darline Graham’s gaffe sufficient to give Norman a chance on Tuesday?: The Hill : “Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Wednesday defended her stumble earlier this week on a national security question during a primary runoff debate, saying she was simply being ‘honest’ about her lack of political experience. ‘I tripped up on one question last night regarding Taiwan,’ Graham said in an interview with Fox News on Wednesday. ‘I have said many times I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician.’ Graham, who was appointed to fill the vacancy left after her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), died last month, was asked during the special GOP debate on Tuesday whether Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the U.S. and why. ‘I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security,’ she responded. ‘But I do support the military.’”

Dems ready to write off Florida Senate race after DSA upset: Politico: “Progressive Angie Nixon ’s stunning upset in Florida’s Senate race has many Democrats in the state spiraling. The Jacksonville lawmaker’s primary victory on Tuesday night over retired Lt. Col. Alexander Vindman jolted a state few thought would hold any surprises. But it also rattled Democrats who worry about her chances against GOP Sen. Ashley Moody in a state that hasn’t picked a Democrat for Senate since 2012. They’re concerned about Nixon’s ability to team up with other candidates and fundraise for down-ballot hopefuls — as Vindman appeared poised to do with his “resistance movement,” Trump-impeachment-era fundraising network. They’re also worried about her more contentious positions, including her decision to join the Democratic Socialists of America in June, in a state where Republicans have 1.5 million more registered voters than Democrats.”

articles.title: ‘Woke’ by any other name: Stop erasing the terms of our survival
articles.summary: Author Andrea D. Pringle argues that while the term “woke” may be evolving in political discourse, the underlying spirit of Black vigilance and awareness remains essential for addressing systemic injustices.
articles.body:
I have watched a word that once helped keep my people alive get turned into a punchline, then a slur, and now, this month, a punchline again, this time by people who are supposed to be on our side.

On Aug. 11, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) sat across from Jonathan Karl on ABC’s “This Week” and, asked about positions held by democratic socialists in 2020, repeated a phrase she attributed to a fellow politician: “ Woke 1 was crazy .” She moved on quickly, arguing reasonably that candidates should be judged on where they stand today rather than where they stood five years ago.

Since then, those four words have become part of a larger debate about what Democrats should leave behind from 2020. Some of that reckoning is overdue. But before we turn “woke” into a convenient label for everything that went wrong, we should remember something important: woke was never a branding exercise for Black people. It was an instruction.

I say that as someone who admires Ocasio-Cortez and the power she has built for working people. This isn’t about piling on. It is about asking who gets to declare a chapter of Black political consciousness embarrassing, close the book and move on. Who gets to decide when our vigilance has become inconvenient? Who gets to gatekeep the language of our survival?

“Woke” did not begin as a hashtag or cable news category. Its roots run through generations of Black political consciousness. Marcus Garvey urged Black people to “wake up” to the reality of their condition. In 1938, Lead Belly sang about the Scottsboro Boys, nine Black teenagers falsely accused in Alabama, and warned Black listeners to “stay woke” and keep their eyes open.

That was the point: Stay alert because the danger is real.

In 1962, novelist William Melvin Kelley wrote in The New York Times about white America’s habit of taking Black vernacular, hollowing it out and handing it back as something unrecognizable. Decades later, Erykah Badu helped return “stay woke” to popular consciousness. Then another generation carried it into the streets after Trayvon Martin, Michael Brown and Eric Garner.

After George Floyd’s murder, the phrase went fully mainstream. Then the right seized it.

Florida eventually put the acronym “WOKE” into the title of legislation restricting certain instruction and workplace training involving race. A phrase rooted in Black vigilance became shorthand for nearly anything conservative politicians wanted their voters to fear. Black Americans have seen this before: Language we create to describe our experience gets stripped of context, weaponized and sold back to the country as something dangerous.

What troubles me now is watching parts of the left participate in a softer version of that erasure.

To be clear, there were real excesses in 2020. Some slogans substituted provocation for persuasion. Some activists treated people who shared the goal of a more just society as enemies because they used imperfect language or asked uncomfortable questions. At times, our desire to create safety for marginalized people produced too little room for people to learn, stumble, apologize and grow.

We should be able to say that. A movement incapable of examining its mistakes is not a movement preparing to win.

But society also needs mechanisms for moving people toward justice collectively. Progress requires persuasion as well as protest, grace as well as accountability. Learning those lessons is very different from declaring the awakening itself “crazy.”

That distinction matters because 2020 did not materialize from an internet trend. Millions of people took to the streets after watching a Black man die beneath a police officer’s knee. They were responding to something real. To dismiss that period as an inconvenient pendulum swing is not politically shortsighted. It risks confusing mistakes made in responding to injustice with the injustice that demanded a response.

And the underlying conditions have not disappeared.

I organize voter registration and civic engagement work across Georgia, South Carolina, Mississippi and Texas. Voter rolls are still purged. Polling places still close. Laws still create barriers for people who move, change their names or lack particular forms of identification. Every day, organizers enter communities that politics has ignored and work to make sure their voices are not erased.

That is what staying woke means to me. It isn’t a vocabulary test or a cable news category. It is the discipline of paying attention because history has taught us who pays the price when we don’t.

I’m not interested in defending a word forever. Language changes, movements mature and political strategies should evolve. If “woke” no longer communicates what we need it to communicate, Black communities can be part of the conversation about what comes next.

But there is a difference between retiring a word and rewriting its history. There is a difference between acknowledging that a movement made mistakes and treating the consciousness that animated it as an embarrassment.

America can change the vocabulary. Politics can find a new slogan. What we cannot afford to discard is the vigilance underneath it, because for generations that vigilance has helped Black Americans recognize danger, organize against injustice and claim rights this country too often tried to deny us.

So rename the word if you must — just don’t try to rename our survival.

Andrea D. Pringle is a Democratic campaigner and founder and president of Registration Nation and leads March On PAC, Elect Southern Dems and Future Democrats. She previously held multiple roles at the Democratic National Committee.

articles.title: What’s with Trump’s war against the US Navy?
articles.summary: So far, the president has insisted that the Navy go back to using steam, decreed that the Strait of Hormuz will be a U.S. territory, and demanded that new aircraft carriers be redesigned to make them look “better.”
articles.body:
August is traditionally silly season for news stories, and President Trump does not disappoint. So far, he has insisted that the Navy go back to using steam , decreed that the Strait of Hormuz will be a U.S. territory , and demanded that new aircraft carriers be redesigned to make them look “better.”

The Hormuz thing is just weird. For one thing, for a country to own a territory, it must permanently physically occupy and control it. You can’t occupy a body of water, and certainly not permanently. Trump’s blockade — which doesn’t actually control the strait — is no help. Eventually, the Fifth Fleet, like the USS Abraham Lincoln , is going to have to sail away, whereas Iran is physically right there and not going anywhere.

More fundamentally, you cannot win a conflict by simply declaring victory. Trump started the Iran war without thinking through the consequences and has painted himself into a corner. That he is “claiming” the Strait of Hormuz rather than wrestling with the very serious problems we now face is a real concern. Perhaps he will next order the U.S. Navy to gather seashells , a la Caligula.

Trump’s fixation on steam catapults for aircraft carriers goes back to his first term. He has now decreed that the new electromagnetic catapults already in use are “ no good ” and that new carriers should go back to steam. It is not entirely clear where all this is coming from, but it is possible that Trump’s analysis is based on the opening scene of “Top Gun.”

It certainly isn’t based on any sort of expertise. In the words of Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), I’ve launched off the front of aircraft carriers hundreds of times, have a Master’s degree in aeronautical engineering, and am a test pilot and even I wouldn’t suggest to the Navy how to engineer specific systems on its ships.” Trump, in contrast, appears to think magnets stop working if they get wet.

If there were a prize for this sort of thing, it would probably go to Trump’s foray into naval architecture. New aircraft carriers have a tower in the back of the ship rather than in the middle like they did in World War 2. The new design allows more planes to take off and land in an hour, making the carrier that much more deadly and effective. But Trump thinks the new design doesn’t look nice, so he is ordering that the tower be moved so that the new carriers look more like they did 80 years ago.

As weird as all this is, none of it is the slightest bit amusing. It is simply further evidence that Trump may be struggling with dementia and that his ability to make rational decisions is decaying by the day .

Worse, these bad decisions are having real consequences, on real people. His efforts to unilaterally redesign American warships just to suit his aesthetic preferences will not only cause delays and cost billions of dollars , it will make those ships less effective when they finally are built. Truly, it’s unforgivable is that the men and women in the U.S. Navy are now suffering because of the foolishness of their commander in chief.

The aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has been deployed for nine months and at sea for more than 200 days, the longest stretch at sea in modern history . The long and unplanned deployment — a direct result of Trump’s poorly conceived war with Iran — has left the ship in terrible condition. There were already food shortages back in April and conditions have only gotten worse . Trump’s response is to call these reports “fake news” and claim that the USS Abraham Lincoln had not really been at sea all that long.

Love him or hate him, you can just imagine what the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) — a real-life war hero — would have had to say about all this. Sadly, backbone and defiance have long been bred out of the current crop of congressional Republicans, so their thunderous silence comes as no surprise. Not only are they not holding the Trump administration to account, some of them are actively defending it. Rep. Pat Fallon (R-Texas), for example, said he didn’t “make much” of the reports about conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln.

Feeding sailors and designing aircraft carriers are not partisan issues. In fact, they are not issues at all — just things that must be properly done. Taking a stand on these things is not asking for much, but apparently it is too much to ask of Republicans. We may have come to expect this kind of cowardice, but we should not accept it.

paragraphs: August is traditionally silly season for news stories, and President Trump does not disappoint. So far, he has insisted that the Navy go back to using steam , decreed that the Strait of Hormuz will be a U.S. territory , and demanded that new aircraft carriers be redesigned to make them look “better.”

The Hormuz thing is just weird. For one thing, for a country to own a territory, it must permanently physically occupy and control it. You can’t occupy a body of water, and certainly not permanently. Trump’s blockade — which doesn’t actually control the strait — is no help. Eventually, the Fifth Fleet, like the USS Abraham Lincoln , is going to have to sail away, whereas Iran is physically right there and not going anywhere.

More fundamentally, you cannot win a conflict by simply declaring victory. Trump started the Iran war without thinking through the consequences and has painted himself into a corner. That he is “claiming” the Strait of Hormuz rather than wrestling with the very serious problems we now face is a real concern. Perhaps he will next order the U.S. Navy to gather seashells , a la Caligula.

Trump’s fixation on steam catapults for aircraft carriers goes back to his first term. He has now decreed that the new electromagnetic catapults already in use are “ no good ” and that new carriers should go back to steam. It is not entirely clear where all this is coming from, but it is possible that Trump’s analysis is based on the opening scene of “Top Gun.”

It certainly isn’t based on any sort of expertise. In the words of Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), I’ve launched off the front of aircraft carriers hundreds of times, have a Master’s degree in aeronautical engineering, and am a test pilot and even I wouldn’t suggest to the Navy how to engineer specific systems on its ships.” Trump, in contrast, appears to think magnets stop working if they get wet.

If there were a prize for this sort of thing, it would probably go to Trump’s foray into naval architecture. New aircraft carriers have a tower in the back of the ship rather than in the middle like they did in World War 2. The new design allows more planes to take off and land in an hour, making the carrier that much more deadly and effective. But Trump thinks the new design doesn’t look nice, so he is ordering that the tower be moved so that the new carriers look more like they did 80 years ago.

As weird as all this is, none of it is the slightest bit amusing. It is simply further evidence that Trump may be struggling with dementia and that his ability to make rational decisions is decaying by the day .

Worse, these bad decisions are having real consequences, on real people. His efforts to unilaterally redesign American warships just to suit his aesthetic preferences will not only cause delays and cost billions of dollars , it will make those ships less effective when they finally are built. Truly, it’s unforgivable is that the men and women in the U.S. Navy are now suffering because of the foolishness of their commander in chief.

The aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln has been deployed for nine months and at sea for more than 200 days, the longest stretch at sea in modern history . The long and unplanned deployment — a direct result of Trump’s poorly conceived war with Iran — has left the ship in terrible condition. There were already food shortages back in April and conditions have only gotten worse . Trump’s response is to call these reports “fake news” and claim that the USS Abraham Lincoln had not really been at sea all that long.

Love him or hate him, you can just imagine what the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) — a real-life war hero — would have had to say about all this. articles.title: The hemp loophole has become a national intoxicant market
articles.summary: An op-ed argues that while recent federal legislation aims to correct the 2018 farm bill’s loophole regarding intoxicating hemp products, states must maintain authority to regulate the burgeoning market to prevent it from becoming politically entrenched.
articles.body:
Congress legalized hemp in 2018 to support American agriculture — not to create a nationwide market for intoxicating gummies, beverages and vaping products. Yet that is precisely what followed.

Businesses exploited the federal definition of hemp to manufacture psychoactive products containing intoxicating cannabinoids. These products quickly migrated from farms and specialized retailers into convenience stores, smoke shops and storefronts across the country.

They are often sold in brightly colored packaging, sometimes resembling ordinary candy or drinks. In many communities, consumers can purchase them without the safeguards traditionally associated with medical or recreational marijuana programs.

The result is a national regulatory failure hiding behind the word “hemp.”

States now face a choice: confront this expanding intoxicant industry or allow it to become economically and politically entrenched. Texas and Arkansas illustrate the consequences of those competing approaches.

In Texas, lawmakers passed Senate Bill 3 to prohibit consumable hemp products containing intoxicating cannabinoids while preserving legitimate non-intoxicating products (such as CBD and CBG). But Gov. Greg Abbott (R) vetoed the legislation . His decision did more than delay a single bill. Texas is the nation’s second-largest state and one of its most valuable consumer markets. By vetoing the prohibition, Abbott gave the intoxicating-hemp industry additional time to open stores, attract customers, hire lobbyists and challenge state regulations in court.

Every year of delay makes reform more difficult. Leases are signed. Trade associations grow. Political contributions increase. Lawyers develop new challenges. What began as the exploitation of a statutory loophole becomes an organized commercial constituency demanding permanent protection.

Arkansas chose a different course. Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R) signed legislation restricting intoxicating hemp-derived products. Businesses sued, and a federal district court initially blocked enforcement.

Arkansas kept fighting, and in 2025, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reversed the injunction in Bio Gen LLC v. Sanders . The appellate court rejected the argument that the 2018 farm bill prevented Arkansas from imposing stronger restrictions. It also rejected the plaintiffs’ vagueness challenge.

The decision does not bind every federal court, including those in Texas. But it demonstrates an important principle with national implications: Congress’s legalization of agricultural hemp did not necessarily strip states of their authority to restrict intoxicating consumer products.

Congress has now acknowledged the underlying problem. Federal legislation enacted in 2025 narrows the definition of lawful hemp by considering total THC content and excluding certain hemp-derived cannabinoid products. Those changes are scheduled to take effect on Nov. 12, 2026 .

That federal correction is welcome, but states should not assume Washington has solved everything.

Questions remain about enforcement, product testing, online sales and the treatment of substances developed to imitate THC’s intoxicating effects. The industry will continue searching for chemical and legal workarounds. Federal agencies will need time to interpret and enforce the new requirements.

Congress should establish a durable national framework that clearly distinguishes agricultural hemp and legitimate non-intoxicating products from recreational intoxicants. States must retain authority to adopt stronger protections suited to their communities.

Lawmakers should also refuse to let veterans become political cover for preserving an inadequately regulated intoxicant market.

I am a disabled veteran who served more than two decades in the Navy, including during the Iraq War. Veterans living with physical injuries and psychological trauma deserve compassionate, evidence-based treatment. If cannabis-derived medicines can help them, those treatments should be evaluated and provided through responsible medical channels.

That is fundamentally different from allowing intoxicating gummies, drinks and vaping products to proliferate in ordinary retail settings.

My years in law enforcement also taught me that preventing substance abuse is far easier than repairing its damage after another intoxicant becomes normalized. Availability matters. Potency matters. Marketing to young consumers matters.

This is no longer a narrow dispute about hemp farming. It is a national debate about whether an unintended loophole should dictate drug policy.

Arkansas demonstrated that a state can defend meaningful restrictions. Texas demonstrated how a governor’s veto can give an expanding industry more time to entrench itself.

Other states — and Congress — should learn from both.

The 2018 farm bill opened a door that lawmakers never intended to open. The country should close it before the intoxicating-hemp market becomes too powerful to control.

Paul Chabot, Ed.D., is president of the Coalition for a Drug Free Texas. He served two U.S. presidents as a White House senior advisor. He is also a retired U.S. Navy intelligence commander, and retired law enforcement officer.

articles.title: Mike Rogers on push for data center pause: ‘Let’s get these questions answered’
articles.summary: Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) is calling for a one-year moratorium on data center construction until Michiganders can “get their questions answered” about such projects. The Republican, who is running in Michigan’s closely watched Senate race, cited his conversations with voters on the campaign trail about the issue in an interview with NewsNation’s Katie Pavlich.…
articles.body:
Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) is calling for a one-year moratorium on data center construction until Michiganders can “get their questions answered” about such projects.

The Republican, who is running in Michigan’s closely watched Senate race , cited his conversations with voters on the campaign trail about the issue in an interview with NewsNation’s Katie Pavlich.

“There is so much concern out there with Michigan citizens,” the former lawmaker, who is backed by President Trump, said. “My argument is that we need to walk through those issues before we just throw these things out.”

The Republican also took a shot at his opponent , Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, saying the progressive “wants to send [the issue] to Washington, D.C., to make the decisions on it.”

“I think that’s a terrible idea,” he continued. “The people who need to make these decisions live in these communities.”

El-Sayed, who is currently leading his GOP opponent in the polls, has proposed several “terms of engagement” for data centers operating in the state on his campaign website .

These rules include restricting energy rate hikes related to data center operations, requiring community input on new projects, ensuring job creation and implementing closed-loop cooling systems to cut down on water pollution.

The pair will face off in the November election to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.). The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election forecaster, rates the contest as a “toss-up.”

Data centers have become a hot topic on campaign trails across the country. Proponents for these projects argue they create jobs and promote AI development, while critics point to their negative impacts on the environment and energy rates.

Earlier this month , Trump criticized Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s (R) decision to impose a moratorium on new data centers in the state.

“I’m not taking positions,” the president told Punchbowl News. “I just think it’s a mistake because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community.”

articles.title: The FDA cannot inspect its way to a safe global food supply
articles.summary: In a country divided on nearly everything, there should be nothing controversial about this: Americans deserve safe food, regardless of where it is produced. The question is how best to ensure it.
articles.body:
Two major outbreaks involving imported produce have again tested Americans’ confidence in the safety of their food. A multistate cyclospora outbreak linked to iceberg lettuce from central Mexico sickened 9,481 people. A salmonella outbreak linked to jalapeño peppers from Sinaloa has sickened 345 people and triggered numerous downstream recalls .

In a country divided on nearly everything, there should be nothing controversial about this: Americans deserve safe food, regardless of where it is produced. The question is how best to ensure it.

Americans expect fresh fruits, vegetables and seafood year-round. Meeting that demand requires importing enormous quantities of food through increasingly complex global supply chains. Our food-safety system needs to adapt .

One longstanding element of the Food and Drug Administration’s imported-food safety strategy relies on a surprisingly old-fashioned approach: sending American investigators around the world to inspect individual foreign food-processing facilities. It is the regulatory equivalent of the Lone Ranger riding into town to handle the problem himself. It is also wildly ineffective.

Congress reinforced that approach with the Food Safety Modernization Act . The foreign-inspection target eventually reached 19,200 facilities annually — a level the FDA itself has called unrealistic and unachievable . The agency has proven itself right many times over.

According to a 2025 Government Accountability Office report, the FDA averaged just 917 foreign food-safety inspections annually from fiscal 2018 through 2023 — less than 5 percent of its target. Even in 2019, when the agency conducted 1,727 inspections, it reached only about 9 percent of the target.

The predictable response is to call for more inspectors, more money and more inspections. But that misses the larger problem. The FDA is relying too heavily on a model that no amount of additional staffing can make scalable.

Imports account for about 15 percent of the U.S. food supply, including 32 percent of fresh vegetables, 55 percent of fresh fruit and 94 percent of seafood. That food comes from more than 200 countries and territories and roughly 125,000 foreign food facilities, plus farms.

Foreign inspections are not the FDA’s only defense. The agency also relies on importer requirements such as the Foreign Supplier Verification Program , along with border screening, examinations, sampling, testing, import alerts and enforcement. Yet Congress continues to emphasize an inspection target bearing little relation to what the FDA can realistically accomplish.

There is another model worth examining. The European Union places substantial reliance on exporting countries and their “competent authorities,” combined with European oversight and risk-based border controls. For many imported foods, exporting countries must demonstrate that their production and control systems comply with EU requirements. Official certificates are issued by the exporting country’s competent authority.

European authorities use audits and other oversight to evaluate national control systems, while border controls provide another layer of protection. The central question is broader than whether one processor complied on the day of an inspection: Does the country’s food-safety control system work?

That is fundamentally different from sending an American investigator overseas primarily to determine whether a single processor complies with U.S. requirements. The U.S. need not copy the European system, but its central principle deserves consideration.

The FDA already recognizes this principle. Its Systems Recognition program evaluates whether other countries operate a comparable food-safety regulatory system and allows the FDA and its foreign counterparts to leverage one another’s regulatory systems and redirect resources based on risk. Yet the FDA currently has Systems Recognition arrangements only with Australia, Canada and New Zealand — countries that already have robust food-safety systems.

Those arrangements can conserve agency resources, but they do relatively little to address the more difficult challenge: ensuring the safety of food coming from major exporting countries where regulatory capacity or compliance may require greater FDA attention.

That is where the greater opportunity lies. The FDA should work with competent authorities in major food-exporting countries to identify weaknesses and strengthen their ability to oversee the farms and processors supplying the U.S. market.

The FDA has already demonstrated how such collaboration can work. In August 2023, it established its first Regulatory Partnership Arrangement with Ecuador for aquacultured shrimp exported to the U.S. The arrangement is designed to leverage Ecuador’s commodity-specific regulatory oversight and allow the governments to exchange information, including inspection records and sampling findings.

Importantly, the FDA itself is now moving in this direction. Its 2026 Human Foods Program priorities explicitly call for the agency to “leverage foreign competent authorities” responsible for food offered for import into the United States. The FDA identifies the Food Safety Partnership with Mexico, Regulatory Partnership Arrangements and Systems Recognition as priorities. For imported shrimp, the FDA says it will advance regulatory partnerships with leading shrimp-exporting countries such as India.

The partnership with Mexico is particularly relevant to the current produce outbreaks. The FDA’s Food Safety Partnership with Mexican agencies grew out of a produce-safety partnership established in 2014 and was expanded in 2020 to cover all FDA-regulated human food. The FDA says that roughly one-third of FDA-regulated human food imported into the U.S. comes from Mexico, including 60 percent of U.S. fresh-produce imports.

Direct FDA inspections remain an important tool, but they should be targeted where they provide the greatest value: high-risk foods, weaker regulatory systems, facilities with poor compliance histories, emerging hazards and verification that foreign authorities are doing their jobs.

For countries with developing food-safety systems, the FDA should combine oversight with technical assistance, training and capacity building. And where governments cannot or will not provide adequate oversight, the FDA should retain its full arsenal of inspections, border examinations, sampling, import alerts and enforcement.

Congress and the FDA should rethink a foreign-inspection strategy built around a numerical target that the FDA itself says is unrealistic. The objective should not be maximizing the number of American inspectors sent overseas but maximizing protection for American consumers.

Brett Koonse worked at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for 31 years as a food-safety official and founded All Things Seafood, LLC.

articles.title: What Trump’s cold shoulder toward South Korea means to our allies
articles.summary: Trump’s coupling of his desire to meet the North Korean dictator with the cutback in joint exercises with South Korea sends the wrong message.
articles.body:
President Trump’s decision to cut roughly in half the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises with South Korea, along with his desire for a fourth meeting with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, has caused considerable consternation among Washington’s key allies in the Far East.

On a visit to Australia, Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi indirectly reflected his unease with Trump’s decision when he stated , “As Japan faces the most severe and complicated security environment in the postwar era, the cooperation among Japan, the U.S. and South Korea is critical to the peace and stability of the region.”

Koizumi’s response to Trump’s action repeated almost verbatim the words of his introduction to the 2026 white paper “Defense of Japan,” in which he added, “In the Indo-Pacific, not only are China and North Korea further strengthening their military capabilities, China-Russia and Russia-North Korea are also reinforcing their cooperation.”

The white paper also stated that “North Korea’s military activities pose an even more grave and imminent threat to Japan’s national security than ever before.”

Koizumi’s Australian host, Richard Marles, said much the same thing, leaving no doubt that Australia has a starkly different view of North Korea from Trump’s. He observed that Canberra “is very concerned about North Korea’s nuclear program as well as its missile program, and we have consistently made that point.” And he termed South Korea “a critically important country,” for his country and for the trilateral relationship among Australia, Japan and South Korea.

Left unstated on the part of both defense ministers was a concern about America’s reliability as an ally. The announcement of the cutback in the U.S.-South Korean exercises follows the redeployment of the aircraft carrier USS George Washington from the Western Pacific to the Middle East, leaving East Asia without an American aircraft carrier presence for the second time since 2024 , when the carrier USS Abraham Lincoln and its battle group first joined the battle group that had already been on station in the Middle East.

With no end in sight to the Iran war, it remains unclear how long there will be no carrier deployed in East Asia. Moreover, it appears that while officially assigning highest priority to East Asia after defense of the American homeland, the redeployment of the carrier to the Middle East is a sign that Washington’s priorities on paper do not match its actual concerns.

China has officially taken a nuanced position regarding the cutback in the joint U.S.-South Korean exercises as well as Trump’s desire to meet yet again with Kim. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jiang simply stated that “maintaining peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and advancing the political settlement of the Korean Peninsula issue serve the common interests of all parties.” Yet surely not coincidentally, only days after Trump’s announcement, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi was to make his first visit to Seoul in five years.

Beijing cannot but view Trump’s announcement with some satisfaction. Indeed, China’s state run media have been considerably less circumspect than the government itself about Trump’s decision reflecting his unhappiness with Seoul’s refusal to support actively the U.S. operation against Iran. The Xinhua News Agency asserted that this is “a stock method the U.S. government uses when pressuring allies … [that] reveals US frustration resulting from policy deadlock on the Korean Peninsula and over Iran.” Xinhua added that “such an alliance system is bound to continuously erode and gradually head toward disintegration.”

China’s view that the American alliance system is beginning to fray is likely premature, but it does have some basis in current reality. Trump’s dissatisfaction with South Korea — and with Japan, for that matter — mirrors his unhappiness with America’s NATO allies. His tariff policy and complaints that European and East Asian allies had not committed sufficient resources for defense preceded the onset of the American operations in the Middle East.

To these prior complaints, Trump has now added criticism of the allies for not actively supporting the ongoing Iran operation.

Trump may rightly feel that any understanding he reaches with Kim will reduce tensions on the Korean Peninsula and in East Asia more generally. But coupling his desire to meet the North Korean dictator again with the cutback in joint exercises with South Korea sends the wrong message both to America’s allies and to Beijing — and Russia, for that matter, which has also become a major Japanese concern .

Even if the current exercises remain truncated, Trump could still elect to let future exercises run their planned course. This would not only reassure nervous allies but also strengthen his hand if his meeting with Kim actually were to take place.

articles.title: ICE begins deporting Haitians who lost temporary protections
articles.summary: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Thursday carried out its first deportation flight to Haiti since the Trump administration terminated deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Haitians earlier this year. The plane, which carried more than 160 people, arrived in the northern Haitian city of Cap-Haïtien, The Associated Press reported. The U.S. has a…
articles.body:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Thursday carried out its first deportation flight to Haiti since the Trump administration terminated deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Haitians earlier this year.

The plane, which carried more than 160 people, arrived in the northern Haitian city of Cap-Haïtien, The Associated Press reported. The U.S. has a ban in place on flights in and out of the country’s main airport in the capital city of Port-au-Prince due to ongoing gang violence.

The deportees on this flight included those previously covered under Temporary Protected Status (TPS), a U.S. program that protects from deportation foreign nationals who cannot safely return to their home country and offers them a pathway to work authorization.

The Supreme Court ruled in June that the Trump administration could end this protection for the around 330,000 Haitians and more than 6,000 Syrians covered by this program.

The administration has looked to terminate deportation protections for migrants from 13 of the 17 countries covered by TPS, arguing that these countries no longer meet the required criteria.

The State Department still lists Haiti as a “ Level 4: Do Not Travel ” country on its travel advisory website, citing gang-related crime, terrorism, unrest and limited healthcare services in the nation. The department also notes Haiti has been under a national state of emergency since 2024.

Immigration activist groups have warned that people deported to Haiti could face dangerous conditions. The U.N. reported that more than 3,100 people were reported killed and 1,189 others were injured in Haiti from January to June.

Haiti’s Group Supporting Refugees and Returnees warned in a Thursday statement the country was “not ready to receive this number of migrants who were in the TPS program.”

articles.title: Building families shouldn’t be this hard
articles.summary: Grindr CEO George Arison and Sen. John Hickenlooper called for federal and state reforms to make fertility care and family formation more accessible and affordable for all Americans.
articles.body:
The deeply personal decision of when and how to build a family has suddenly become part of a national conversation. At the heart of this conversation is the profound hope held by millions of Americans: to one day hold one’s own child for the first time.

For each of us, that moment came after years of uncertainty, hope, and extraordinary help from others. Our paths were different, but they led to the same realization: You are not free if you don’t have the freedom to decide when and how to have a family.

One of us welcomed a son after doctors said there was only a one-in-a-million chance of conceiving without in vitro fertilization. The other became a father to two children through surrogacy after nearly three years of navigating the financial, legal and emotional complexities of the process.

Those experiences changed us and made one thing abundantly clear: For too many Americans, becoming a parent is far more difficult than it should be.

No one should have to win the financial or legal lottery to become a parent. Yet today’s system is too often defined by staggering costs, outdated policies and unnecessary legal uncertainty. Families and same-sex couples spend years navigating barriers that have little to do with medicine and everything to do with bureaucracy or politics. That should change.

If we are serious about strengthening families, growing our economy, and investing in the next generation, we should be making it easier for Americans to become parents.

This is not a Democratic issue or a Republican issue, it’s an American one. When Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) shared her experience navigating the costly and complicated fertility care system , the response cut across the usual dividing lines with praise from conservative and progressive media personalities. As a nation, we disagree on many things. But we agree that having a family is a gift and a right, and our system should make it both accessible and affordable for all.

Fortunately, the solutions don’t require reinventing the system. They require modernizing it. Congress and the administration should focus on three practical reforms.

First, make fertility-related expenses — including in-vitro fertilization and surrogacy — fully tax deductible for all Americans seeking to start a family. Families routinely spend tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars pursuing parenthood. Those costs should be treated like the essential medical and family-building expenses they are.

Second, modernize federal insurance rules so that employers can more easily offer comprehensive fertility and surrogacy benefits. While some insurance plans cover portions of IVF, coverage for the medical care associated with surrogacy remains inconsistent or nonexistent.

Updating federal guidance would give employers greater flexibility to support employees who rely on assisted reproductive technology to build their families. One of us runs a company whose employees are eligible for up to $300,000 in family formation support that can go towards IVF, surrogacy and adoption. Public policy should make it easier for other employers to follow suit.

Third, states should follow Colorado’s lead and pass clear parentage laws, including orders that let intended parents establish their legal rights before the baby is even born. That way, when a child arrives, there is no question about who his or her legal parents are. No family should begin one of its happiest days facing avoidable legal confusion.

Federal policy should also adopt the modern medical definition of infertility that recognizes infertility is not defined solely by months of unsuccessful attempts to conceive, but by a person’s inability to achieve a successful pregnancy based on their full medical, sexual and reproductive history. That would ensure today’s policies reflect today’s science and today’s families.

These ideas are already gaining traction across the country.

Colorado and California have demonstrated that thoughtful reforms can expand access to fertility care while supporting families. George was proud to support California’s landmark expansion of in vitro insurance coverage , and employers are increasingly recognizing that helping employees build families is both good policy and good business.

Like all Americans, our stories are different. Our politics are not identical. But parenthood has a way of clarifying priorities. Every parent who dreams of raising a child should have a fair opportunity to pursue that dream.

This should not be controversial. It should be one of the easiest decisions we make for a better America.

George Arison is chairman and CEO of Grindr Inc. John Hickenlooper (D) is a father to two sons and the junior U.S. senator from Colorado.

articles.title: Massie, Greene slam Trump’s move to lower beef prices
articles.summary: Two Republicans pushed back on the Trump administration’s Friday decision to temporarily lift certain tariffs on imported ground beef in an effort to bring down prices for American consumers ahead of the midterm elections. President Trump announced in a Truth Social post Friday morning that he had finalized “a deal to substantially lower the price…
articles.body:
Two Republicans pushed back on the Trump administration’s Friday decision to temporarily lift certain tariffs on imported ground beef in an effort to bring down prices for American consumers ahead of the midterm elections.

President Trump announced in a Truth Social post Friday morning that he had finalized “a deal to substantially lower the price of ground beef for working American families.”

The president said his administration will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of ground beef to be imported without an “out-of-quota tariff” in the next 90 days.

The imported product would be sold at 25 percent below market price — a move Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie (R) called a “slap in the face to American cattlemen & consumers.”

“Worse than socialism! Dumping foreign beef in U.S. markets can temporarily lower prices but it won’t incentivize American farmers to raise more beef,” Massie wrote on social media .

The GOP lawmaker urged the Trump administration to bring back labels indicating which countries products were imported from and called on Congress to pass his Processing Revival and Intrastate Meat Exemption (PRIME) Act .

The PRIME Act would permit states to allow farmers and ranchers to slaughter their livestock at local slaughterhouses and reduce reliance on the select meat processing centers approved by the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

Former GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (Ga.) also joined in on criticizing the move, accusing the Trump administration of “making it even harder for American beef ranchers and producers.”

“Now they will be undercut by foreign imported beef, as they have been hit financially with high cost of fertilizer and diesel from Trump’s war with Iran,” Greene wrote in a Friday social media post . “The Trump admins attempt to lower the cost of beef is American beef LAST and foreign beef FIRST.”

A historically small U.S. cattle herd and high consumer demand has driven up the domestic cost of ground beef.

The average price of 100 percent ground beef per pound was around $6.89 in July — a more than 10 percent increase from a year ago, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data shared by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis .

Trump said Friday the new move will “reduce prices for Americans while giving space for our Great American Beef Herd to grow again.”

articles.title: ‘Who knows?’: Jill Biden responds to theory Joe Biden was drugged before debate
articles.summary: I don’t think the lesson here is that Jill Biden should never talk about her husband’s presidency. She absolutely has a right to tell her story. But you cannot rewrite history, no matter how many times you try.
articles.body:
Everyone remembers that disastrous presidential debate then President Biden had against Donald Trump in 2024. It was so jarring that it ultimately helped end his reelection campaign. And now, nearly two years later, former first lady Jill Biden is once again talking about what happened that night — including whether her husband could have been drugged.

She made the comments during an appearance on “The Jamie Kern Lima Show.” Asked if he was “having a stroke or — uh, uh, was he drugged? Were there any steps taken after to rule out?” Jill Biden answered, “Oh, yeah. Either.”

“I mean, Joe and I both had a team of doctors around both of us at all times, and he had a team, I had a team. … And yeah, they checked him out. I mean, once we got off the stage, I went to the green room to get my, my pocketbook and all that stuff, and he went to his staff and the docs and, um, and they said, ‘Jill, he’s fine. He’s OK.’”

So here’s where I think we need to separate what we know from what we still don’t know.

We know Joe Biden had an extraordinarily poor debate performance. We know Jill Biden says she immediately noticed that he did not seem like himself. And we know his doctors examined him afterward, according to her, and told her he was OK.

What we do not have is evidence that Joe Biden was drugged. But when asked about the possibility that someone could have put something in his drink , she said, “Who knows? Who knows?”

And that’s the problem with continuing to elevate that possibility: “Who knows?” is not evidence.

In her memoir, “View from the East Wing,” Jill Biden herself describes the fear and confusion she felt watching the debate. She wrote that she wondered, “Is this a stroke?” and even asked herself, “Has he been drugged?” She has said she still doesn’t know what happened that night.

Joe Biden was 81 years old. The debate intensified already existing concerns about his age and ability to serve another four years. He ultimately ended his reelection campaign less than a month later.

The Democratic Party has to be honest. There have been serious questions about whether Biden’s age and health were adequately confronted inside his political circle. The 2025 book “Original Sin,” by Jake Tapper and Alex Thompson, argued that Biden’s inner circle shielded him from difficult information and that concerns about his decline were minimized. The first lady is depicted as a central figure in hiding that from public view.

So I don’t think the lesson here is that Jill Biden should never talk about her husband’s presidency. She absolutely has a right to tell her story. But you cannot rewrite history, no matter how many times you try.

And nearly two years later, the Democratic Party still has to reckon with the consequences of that debate — not because Trump needs another villain, and not because Joe Biden needs another defense, but because voters deserve political leaders who can acknowledge what went wrong without searching for a mystery explanation that has never been substantiated.

Joe Biden is now battling stage 4 prostate cancer that has spread to his bones , according to his son. Jill Biden has spoken publicly about the toll that diagnosis has taken on their family and about trying to make the most of the time they have together. One way to help both Biden’s legacy and Democrats’ future chances is to stop pretending and stop relitigating the past. At that point, the party may learn from it and finally be able to move forward.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Trump’s move to pause beef tariffs risks blowback
articles.summary: 😎 Plus: South Carolina gets a dose of Trump {beacon} It’s Friday. Against all odds and several hundred emails, we’ve made it. In today’s issue: Beef tariffs get a timeout Bessent weighs America’s debt Trump goes all in for Graham IndyCar zooms into DC Programming note: Hello! We are Colin Meyn and Steff…
articles.body:
It’s Friday. Against all odds and several hundred emails , we’ve made it.

Programming note : Hello! We are Colin Meyn and Steff Danielle Thomas filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to cmeyn@thehill.com or sthomas@thehill.com .

President Trump is intervening in the beef markets in a move certain to irk some key constituencies.

What’s the deal? In a Truth Social post , Trump said, “for the next 90 days, the United States will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported with no out of quota tariff. We have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices.”

The president did not say where the beef is coming from, but he has previously considered similar arrangements with Argentina.

Beef prices have risen faster than other foods during Trump’s second term. Both ground beef and beef steak pieces rose by 9 percent or more year-on-year, according to the July CPI report .

Queue the blowback: Trump’s previous meddling in the beef market has drawn criticism from cattle ranchers and Republican senators in major beef-producing states.

Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.), a staunch Trump ally, said Friday in a post on social platform X that he’d been warning against such action “because American ranchers have been struggling against the packer monopoly for decades, and this will further harm them — most of whom are MAGA Republicans.”

Other criticism came from some predictable figures.

“What a slap in the face to American cattlemen & consumers,” Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) wrote online . “Worse than socialism! Dumping foreign beef in U.S. markets can temporarily lower prices but it won’t incentivize American farmers to raise more beef.”

Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) chimed in too , saying U.S. farmers will now “be undercut by foreign imported beef, as they have been hit financially with high cost of fertilizer and diesel from Trump’s war with Iran.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is scrambling to convince the markets to stop selling off U.S. bonds.

He moved on Wednesday to double the Treasury’s buyback limit, and on Thursday went on CNBC to declare he was ready to intervene further if needed.

But bond yields only moved higher Thursday, after ticking down Wednesday. The 30-year bond yield, a key indicator of economic health, remained above 5.25 percent on Friday, as high as it’s been since before the global recession in 2008.

Tell me more about this bond yield: Sure. It’s basically how much interest the government has to pay on future bonds it issues. When investors are feeling good about the economy, yields are low because demand is high. When investors are feeling anxious, yields go up to help them hedge against risk.

Bessent told CNBC he’s got more tricks up his sleeve while arguing the markets are misreading America’s economic strength.

The president did not say where the beef is coming from, but he has previously considered similar arrangements with Argentina.

articles.title: Watch live: Vance seeks to sell Trump agenda to Ohio voters
articles.summary: Vice President Vance is heading back to his Ohio hometown Friday afternoon, as he looks to sell President Trump’s economic agenda to voters ahead of the November midterms. Vance will deliver remarks at Cleveland-Cliffs Middletown Works, a steel plant where his grandfather worked for nearly four decades. He is expected to tout the administration’s efforts…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance is heading back to his Ohio hometown Friday afternoon, as he looks to sell President Trump’s economic agenda to voters ahead of the November midterms.

Vance will deliver remarks at Cleveland-Cliffs Middletown Works, a steel plant where his grandfather worked for nearly four decades. He is expected to tout the administration’s efforts to boost domestic manufacturing and will be joined by Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

The stop comes as Republicans face increasingly competitive races in the Buckeye State. Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who was appointed to fill Vance’s former Senate seat, is facing former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), while Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is running against Democrat Amy Acton for governor.

The event in Middletown, Ohio, is scheduled to begin at 1 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: Trump lawyer to liberal think tank: Retract National Guard report that defames president
articles.summary: President Trump has demanded a liberal think tank retract a critical report on his National Guard deployments by Friday evening, threatening to file a $5 billion defamation suit if it doesn’t. In a nine-page letter sent Monday by Trump’s personal attorney, which was reviewed by The Hill, he claimed the Center for American Progress (CAP) “manufactured”…
articles.body:
President Trump has demanded a liberal think tank retract a critical report on his National Guard deployments by Friday evening, threatening to file a $5 billion defamation suit if it doesn’t.

In a nine-page letter sent Monday by Trump’s personal attorney, which was reviewed by The Hill, he claimed the Center for American Progress (CAP) “manufactured” that the deployments weren’t improving violent crime.

“Defendants did not merely draw a different academic conclusion; they defamed President Trump by distorting a contested empirical question into a sensational, false, malicious and defamatory accusation that President Trump knowingly lied to the American people,” attorney Alejandro Brito wrote.

In a statement, CAP President and CEO Neera Tanden, a senior adviser to former President Biden, called the threat “baseless” and defended the report as “rigorous, evidence-based research and analysis.”

“A fundamental protection of the First Amendment is to allow for the publication of facts and analysis that are contrary to the arguments and claims of any administration. A lawsuit is a transparent attempt to silence us. We will neither cower nor bend in the face of it,” she said.

“In America, profound disagreements over public policy are resolved through robust public debate, not through threats or intimidation,” the statement continued. “Independent data, evidence, and analysis are essential to that debate. Efforts to silence independent research because its findings are unwelcome by an administration or president should alarm every American.”

During his presidency, Trump’s personal lawyers have advanced a handful of defamation suits against those he perceives as foes. Often brought against media organizations with demands for 10-figure sums, Trump’s lawsuits have at times prompted significant settlements.

His latest threat targets Tanden’s think tank and other senior officials in past Democratic administrations on the board.

CAP drew Trump’s ire for publishing a report last month saying there was “no evidence” the president’s National Guard deployments reduced violent crime. The group accused the administration of trying to take credit for a trend that was already underway to justify expanding policing.

“How crazy is that,” Trump wrote on Truth Social earlier this month, threatening legal action as he called the report “another Radical Left SCAM.”

The letter, which was first reported by The New York Times , escalates the president’s public threat, with a timeline. Brito set a 5 p.m. EDT Friday deadline for CAP to retract the report, apologize and compensate Trump or risk facing an at least $5 billion suit.

“Failure to comply will leave President Trump with no choice but to pursue any and all legal rights and remedies available to recover damages for the overwhelming financial and reputational harm that Defendants have caused him to suffer,” the letter states.

Kevin H. Metz, CAP’s general counsel, sent a written response Friday to Trump’s lawyer calling any suit “absurd.” He warned that if Trump follows through, the group would welcome full discovery detailing the costs of the National Guard deployments and the “full picture” of White House involvement.

Metz also warned that threatening the group could ultimately hurt conservative groups, too.

“Such a precedent would not stay confined to CAP, and the next administration could just as easily target the Heritage Foundation or America First Policy Institute for facts they report that the president finds inconvenient,” Metz wrote. “That would be wrong and indeed unAmerican, just as this threat of litigation is.”
