articles.title: Sanford backs Norman over Graham in South Carolina Senate runoff: ‘Stakes are simply too high’
articles.summary: Former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford (R) announced Friday he is backing GOP Rep. Ralph Norman (S.C.) in the race to serve a full term in the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R-S.C.) seat. Sanford, who generally refrains from offering political endorsements, said in a statement shared on social media that he felt “compelled to offer”…
articles.body:
Former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford (R) announced Friday he is backing GOP Rep. Ralph Norman (S.C.) in the race to serve a full term in the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R-S.C.) seat.

Sanford, who generally refrains from offering political endorsements, said in a statement shared on social media that he felt “compelled to offer” his perspective in the race after the national debt hit $40 trillion this week.

“As much as I would like to honor tradition and old friendships, the stakes are simply too high as our nation really is at a financial tipping point,” the former governor said. “It’s for these reasons and more that I will be voting for Ralph on Tuesday and respectfully ask that you do the same.”

Sanford’s endorsement comes ahead of the GOP primary runoff next Tuesday between Norman and Graham’s sister, Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who was tapped to serve out the remainder of the late senator’s term.

The race advanced to a runoff after neither candidate secured a majority of the vote in the state’s Republican primary last week.

Sanford ran in the GOP primary to replace Lindsey Graham and came in fourth place.

Norman said he was “honored” to receive the former state official’s support in the race in a Friday statement.

“The Senate has become a place where good legislation goes to die, and as we elect our next U.S. Senator, we NEED a PROVEN conservative to take up the mantle and fight!” he wrote in a social media post. “I’m the only candidate in this race with the experience and the resume to take on this job, and I look forward to representing the Palmetto State in the United States Senate!”

Sanford noted in his lengthy endorsement message that his “prayers continue to go out to Darline Graham” following the death of her brother.

“I know her to be a good lady and my relationship to her late brother, her staff and many of her supporters had me wanting to do as I had done so many times before and stay neutral in this race,” he wrote.

Sanford’s endorsement follows a rocky week for Darline Graham after she fumbled a question during a debate against Norman about the importance of Taiwan and the South China Sea to U.S. national security.

“I’m just going to be honest here … I’m not that informed on national security,” Graham responded, before adding, “But I do support the military.”

Graham is backed by President Trump and other prominent Republicans, including Sen. Tim Scott (S.C.) and the state’s lieutenant governor, Pamela Evette.

Trump is scheduled to participate in a campaign rally for Graham in Myrtle Beach, S.C., on Friday.

articles.title: North Carolina Senate race between Cooper, Whatley tightens: Poll
articles.summary: Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper (D) is maintaining his lead over former Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Michael Whatley in the state’s Senate race, according to a new poll released Friday. A High Point University Poll found the Democratic candidate had a 5-point advantage over his GOP opponent among likely North Carolina voters. Fifty…
articles.body:
Former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper (D) is maintaining his lead over former Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Michael Whatley in the state’s Senate race, according to a new poll released Friday.

A High Point University Poll found the Democratic candidate had a 5-point advantage over his GOP opponent among likely North Carolina voters. Fifty percent of respondents backed Cooper, while 45 percent supported Whatley in the contest.

The candidates will face off in the November race to replace retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis. The North Carolina seat is one of the six GOP-controlled seats Democrats are hoping to flip this election cycle.

Democrats are currently at a 53-47 disadvantage in the Senate and would need to flip at least four seats to gain control of the upper legislative chamber.

The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election observer, shifted its forecast in the North Carolina race from a “toss-up” to “leans Democratic” in April, following a trend in polling favoring the former governor.

The battleground state narrowly supported President Trump in the past three presidential elections.

This latest survey shows the former RNC chair polling in closer range to his Democratic opponent than in previous polling.

A poll released earlier this month from Carolina Forward found Cooper had a 7-point advantage over Whatley. Support was largely split along partisan lines, with 97 percent of Democratic respondents supporting the former governor and 91 percent of Republicans backing the former RNC chair in this survey.

Cooper had a nearly 13-point advantage over Whatley in a Carolina Journal poll released last week, receiving 52 percent support among likely voters in the state. Thirty-nine percent of respondents supported the Republican candidate in this survey.

The High Point University poll surveyed a sample of 660 likely North Carolina voters from Aug. 3 to 12. The results had a margin of error of approximately 5.2 percentage points.

articles.title: Chief Justice Roberts briefly allows White House ballroom construction
articles.summary: Chief Justice John Roberts temporarily blocked a ruling that was set to halt construction on the White House ballroom later Friday, ruling that work can briefly continue as the Supreme Court mulls the Trump administration’s emergency plea to intervene. It delays, for now, a lower court’s deadline to stop above-ground construction by the end of the day. …
articles.body:
Chief Justice John Roberts temporarily blocked a ruling that was set to halt construction on the White House ballroom later Friday, ruling that work can briefly continue as the Supreme Court mulls the Trump administration’s emergency plea to intervene.

It delays, for now, a lower court’s deadline to stop above-ground construction by the end of the day.

Roberts’s order gives the Supreme Court additional time to consider the administration’s emergency appeal but contains no explanation. It does not necessarily reflect the court’s thinking on the underlying legal issues.

The chief justice received the appeal because he handles emergency matters arising from the nation’s capital by default. He could still refer it to the full court for a vote, as is typical in appeals brought by the Justice Department.

The Justice Department asserts that the project must continue for security reasons after a series of shootings and threats in President Trump’s vicinity.

The 90,000-square-foot project has been challenged by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which convinced the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that the ballroom required additional congressional authorization.

“If Petitioners believe there is a pressing need for a ballroom, nothing prevents them from asking Congress for one — today, tomorrow, or any time in the future,” the group, represented by Foley Hoag, wrote in court filings. “But Petitioners’ efforts to foil judicial review and arrogate Congress’s exclusive powers should not be rewarded.”

The Hill has reached out to spokespeople for the group’s legal team and the Justice Department for comment.

The Trump administration argues the project has the needed approvals because it uses private funds. It also argues the preservationist group has no right to sue over it in court.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices “that would open the courthouse doors to any of the millions of people who visit government buildings, historic sites, or parks and happen to think that they dislike something they see.”

A new ruling on the ballroom could come at any time.

The Supreme Court is simultaneously weighing the Trump administration’s emergency plea to enforce his executive order targeting mail voting in time for the midterms.

articles.title: GOP backlash grows to Trump’s beef price intervention
articles.summary: GOP lawmakers and cattle ranchers are immediately raising alarm bells over President Trump’s decision to temporarily lift certain tariffs on imported ground beef to mitigate the cost for American consumers. The president said Friday a deal is coming that would lower the price of ground beef for Americans to 25 percent below the current market…
articles.body:
GOP lawmakers and cattle ranchers are immediately raising alarm bells over President Trump’s decision to temporarily lift certain tariffs on imported ground beef to mitigate the cost for American consumers.

The president said Friday a deal is coming that would lower the price of ground beef for Americans to 25 percent below the current market price. It failed to say from which country the beef would be imported.

Critics say that while keeping prices affordable for Americans is important, it shouldn’t be done at the expense of American cattle ranchers.

“While America’s cattle producers share the goal of keeping groceries affordable for consumers, flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd,” Colin Woodall, CEO of the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, said in a statement. “Cattle markets have already turned sharply lower this morning, to the detriment of farmers and ranchers.”

“This is a critical time of year for cattle producers, as we approach the season where they are making decisions regarding their herds,” he added. “Cattle farmers and ranchers are responding to strong market signals and historically high demand, and we are already working to rebuild after years of ongoing drought, high input costs and other challenges that have reduced U.S. cattle numbers.”

He said the announcement throws “cold water” on the idea of expanding herds.

Meriwether Farms, a farm-to-table cattle operation from Wyoming, called the president’s actions a “betrayal” on social media.

Trump said the temporarily lifted tariffs would last for 90 days to allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported “as we work to rebuild this herd and help our ranchers.”

The president planned a similar move in May, according to Politico, but shelved the idea after pushback from his inner circle.

“Beef prices are elevated because of supply shortages that began under the Biden administration – the American cattle herd size is at a multi-decade low, while domestic demand for beef continues to be high,” a White House official said. “This short-term action allows foreign imports to fill a gap to meet domestic ground beef demand at affordable prices.”

Rep. Kat Cammack (R-Fla.) said that ranchers from her state will “feel this squeeze, and they deserve a long-term plan that doesn’t leave them in limbo.”

“President Trump is right to make lowering grocery costs for American families a priority. I share his commitment to bringing those costs down,” she wrote on social platform X. “At the same time, short-term relief can’t come at the expense of American ranchers, free markets and long-term solutions. American ranchers have battled drought, rising input costs, and an out-of-control regulatory system that makes it harder and more expensive to produce here at home.”

Beef prices have been soaring across the country. The average price of 100 percent ground beef per pound in the U.S. is roughly $6.89, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data shared by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis .

The prices have increased because the U.S. is facing record-low cattle numbers due to several factors, including droughts and rising operational costs, all the while demand remains high.

Data from the Department of Agriculture showed that the U.S. started with 86.2 million cattle at the beginning of the year, the lowest cattle inventory since 1951 .

“I’ve advised President Trump against this course of action for a year because American ranchers have been struggling against the packer monopoly for decades, and this will further harm them – most of whom are MAGA Republicans,” Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) wrote on X.

“The reality is this action will make it more difficult for American ranchers to rebuild our herd and bring prices down for the American people,” he added. “And most importantly, this will harm our ranching families who feed the nation.”

Supporters of Trump have even weighed in to hit on this decision.

Fox News’s Tomi Lahren said on social media that “if this is the plan the VERY LEAST that can be done is mandatory country of origin labeling so consumers know where the beef they’re buying is coming from.”

“Importing a bunch of foreign beef is just a giant gift to the meat packers who then get to undercut our American ranchers who cannot differentiate their product from the cheap foreign s‑‑‑,” she said. “The American cattlemen is being driven out of business so the land can be gobbled up for data centers and other bulls‑‑‑.”

Critics also said the move shows that Trump’s use of tariffs hurts Americans.

“Trump is once again explicitly admitting his broad-based tariffs raise prices for Americans — and it’s true from groceries to back-to-school shopping to buying a new home,” Alex Jacquez, senior vice president of policy, advocacy and research at Groundwork Collaborative, said in a statement.

Marian Tupy, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute, said the measure “once again exposes the absence of a coherent economic philosophy within MAGA.”

“The principle seems to change with the president’s policy,” he said. “When Trump imposes tariffs, his defenders insist that they do not raise prices for American consumers. When Trump cuts tariffs, many of the same defenders celebrate the move because it will lower prices for American consumers. Both claims cannot be true at the same time.”

“The simplest explanation is that loyalty to Trump comes first and the economic rationale follows,” he added.

articles.title: Appeals court affirms top federal prosecutor in Albany ‘not lawfully serving’
articles.summary: A federal appeals court panel ruled Friday that John Sarcone was “not lawfully serving” as the top federal prosecutor in upstate New York when he subpoenaed New York Attorney General Letitia James’s (D) office last year. The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Sarcone’s January disqualification as the acting U.S. attorney for the Northern…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court panel ruled Friday that John Sarcone was “not lawfully serving” as the top federal prosecutor in upstate New York when he subpoenaed New York Attorney General Letitia James’s (D) office last year.

The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Sarcone’s January disqualification as the acting U.S. attorney for the Northern District of New York in a 2-1 decision, affirming a lower court order that also quashed the subpoenas.

The ruling is yet another blow to the Justice Department’s efforts to test the limits of federal vacancy law and bypass Senate confirmation.

“We hold that Sarcone was not serving as Acting U.S. Attorney when he obtained the subpoenas because the FVRA permits only a First Assistant already in place when the vacancy arises to become the acting officer automatically,” Judge Guido Calabresi wrote in a 39-page opinion, using an abbreviation for the Federal Vacancies Reform Act.

Calabresi, a Clinton nominee, was joined in the majority by the Biden-appointed Judge Maria Araújo Kahn. Judge Michael Park, nominated during President Trump’s first term, dissented.

A spokesperson for the Justice Department told The Hill on Friday that they disagree with the court’s decision and “intend to take this case to the Supreme Court.”

The FVRA states the first assistant to any Senate-confirmed officer assumes the acting role by default whenever a vacancy occurs.

The Trump administration has sought to leverage the automatic succession rule to install top federal prosecutors by designating individuals as first assistants — the No. 2 role in U.S. attorney’s offices — or, in some cases, simply delegating them the powers of the job.

But the 2nd Circuit majority found both of those maneuvers to be unlawful.

“To install someone in a vacant office through a general delegation authority that [federal statute] expressly forbids, is to install an acting officer by another name,” Calabresi noted. “The FVRA forbids it.”

After Sarcone’s 120-day term as interim U.S. attorney expired last July, district judges in New York declined to appoint him to the role indefinitely. Then-Attorney General Pam Bondi subsequently changed his title to “special attorney,” allowing him to remain in the acting position.

Last August, Sarcone subpoenaed James’s office for information about its civil fraud investigation into Trump and his business and another case involving the National Rifle Association.

U.S. District Judge Lorna Schofield blocked the subpoenas in January and disqualified Sarcone, finding that the Justice Department’s workaround violated federal law.

Park disagreed with Friday’s ruling, arguing in a 24-page dissent that Sarcone was legally authorized to seek the grand jury subpoenas.

“By concluding otherwise, the majority imposes new limits on executive authority, upsetting the balance that Congress struck in the FVRA,” the Trump appointee wrote.

The 2nd Circuit’s decision follows a series of recent appeals court rulings that have invalidated the Trump’s administration’s attempts to install loyalists as lead federal prosecutors in California, Nevada, New Jersey and elsewhere.

articles.title: Controversial attorney Ed Martin leaving Justice Department
articles.summary: The head of the Justice Department’s Weaponization Working Group, Ed Martin, is leaving the department, capping a chaotic tenure in the Trump administration. Martin, who also served as the U.S. pardon attorney, has been at the center of a string of controversies since the earliest days of joining the administration, including failing to advance as a nominee…
articles.body:
The head of the Justice Department’s Weaponization Working Group, Ed Martin, is leaving the department, capping a chaotic tenure in the Trump administration.

Martin, who also served as the U.S. pardon attorney, has been at the center of a string of controversies since the earliest days of joining the administration, including failing to advance as a nominee for U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia.

“Ed Martin has been with me from the very beginning, and done an incredible job as an Attorney, Director of the Weaponization Working Group, and the United States Attorney for the District of Columbia,” President Trump wrote on Truth Social in announcing the departure.

“Ed is now leaving to go outside to fight Legal Battles for the upcoming Midterm Election, and the Presidential Election of 2028. I know he will do an outstanding job, ensure Free, Fair, and Honest Elections, and strongly advance our Constitutional Rights.”

“Proud to serve. Fight Fight Fight,” Martin wrote on the social platform X in response to the news.

Martin failed to gain the support of Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) because he represented numerous clients who stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021.

While serving as acting U.S. attorney while his nomination was pending, Martin moved to dismiss some cases of clients — sparking calls for an inquiry into the apparent conflict of interest by the D.C. Bar that has since been taken up by its Office of Professional Responsibility.

“By not recusing himself from this matter, Mr. Martin created an impermissible conflict of interest and appearance of impropriety by using his new government office to favor his client, whom he was defending from the very charges he sought to dismiss,” wrote Sen. Dick Durbin (Ill.), the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, in a 2025 letter requesting an ethics investigation.

Martin made a number of notable moves in just a few months in the acting role, such as sending letters to two sitting Democratic lawmakers informing them they were under investigation for past comments he alleged were threatening, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.).

He also sent a letter to Georgetown University saying he would not hire any interns or attorneys from the school if they did not end its diversity, equity and inclusion policies, later escalating that threat by saying failure to respond would “bear directly” on its nonprofit status. That matter is also under investigation .

After any route to confirmation in the Senate collapsed, Martin was then moved to his dual role at the Department of Justice (DOJ).

He took the job of Liz Oyer, the prior U.S. pardon attorney, who was fired after refusing to recommend actor Mel Gibson have his gun rights restored.

Under Martin, Trump pardoned a number of people who donated to his campaign or affiliated entities or who otherwise were allies.

In a Friday report titled “Pardon Inc.,” Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, accused Trump of effectively selling pardons.

“Mr. Martin has since described his philosophy as ‘No MAGA left behind’ and has used his office to privilege clemency applications from the Oath Keepers, the Proud Boys, and the two men convicted of plotting to kidnap Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer,” the panel wrote in its report.

“Convicted investor fraudster Trevor Milton and his wife donated more than $1.8 million to committees supporting Trump before Milton hired two attorneys with direct Trump ties and received a full pardon; tax fraudster Paul Walczak received a pardon 12 days after his mother attended a $1 million-per-plate Trump fundraiser offering face time with the President; and Binance founder Changpeng Zhao hired a longtime friend of Donald Trump, Jr. to lobby for clemency as Binance developed extensive financial ties to the Trump family’s cryptocurrency business before Trump pardoned him,” the report states.

Martin was also scrutinized for a third role he played at the DOJ as a special attorney for mortgage fraud.

A federal grand jury was empaneled in Maryland that took the highly unusual step of launching a probe into one of its own investigations — its review into mortgage fraud allegations against Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.).

A subpoena reviewed by The Hill asked a witness whether they dealt with anyone “claiming to be working for or at the direction” of the Justice Department, including Martin. Other outlets reported prosecutors were evaluating whether Martin may have wrongly deputized two figures outside the DOJ to aid in the investigation of Schiff.

Attorney General Todd Blanche noted Martin’s exit on Friday.

“Ed Martin is a patriot who loves this nation. We thank him for his service to the Department, @POTUS and the American people. We look forward to seeing his future successes!” he wrote on X.

articles.body:
President Trump on Friday sought to ease price pressure on beef prices by temporarily lifting the tariffs on imported beef. The move drew swift and sharp rebukes from some lawmakers and ranchers.

Trump is set to hit the campaign trail Friday in an attempt to give Republican Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.) one last boost before the special GOP primary runoff Tuesday.

Graham, a political newcomer who replaced her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), is going up against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) for the opportunity to snag the Republican seat in the Palmetto State.

Darline Graham’s inexperience showed on the debate stage Tuesday when she was unable to answer a national security question, raising uncertainty about her ability to serve in the Senate.

The Supreme Court on Friday temporarily halted an appeals court order that would’ve stopped above-ground construction on the White House ballroom. Chief Justice John Roberts’s administrative stay gives the court additional time to consider the administration’s emergency appeal but contains no explanation. It does not necessarily reflect the court’s thinking on the underlying legal issues.

IndyCar will take over the District of Columbia this weekend, with the Freedom 250 race Saturday and Sunday. It may cause a “little bit of carnage,” the IndyCar chief said.

articles.title: Appeals court slashes Alex Jones’s Sandy Hook judgment from $50M to $1.5M
articles.summary: A Texas court on Friday cut the amount Infowars founder Alex Jones was ordered to pay to a family affected by the Sandy Hook shooting after they were subject to harassment when he claimed the attack was a hoax. The Texas 3rd Court of Appeals ruled unanimously to reduce the damages awarded to Neil Heslin…
articles.body:
A Texas court on Friday cut the amount Infowars founder Alex Jones was ordered to pay to a family affected by the Sandy Hook shooting after they were subject to harassment when he claimed the attack was a hoax.

The Texas 3rd Court of Appeals ruled unanimously to reduce the damages awarded to Neil Heslin and Scarlett Lewis from more than $45 million to $1.5 million, according to court documents .

“The Court modifies the trial court’s judgment by reducing the exemplary damages award consistent with the statutory cap, resulting in exemplary damages awards of $750,000 to Scarlett Lewis and of $750,000 to Neil Heslin,” Chief Justice of the 3rd Court of Appeals of Texas Darlene Byrne wrote in her opinion Friday.

It found that there was no evidence that showed the harassment the couple endured from the claims Jones made allowed for the cap to be exceeded.

The ruling did not touch the $4.1 million Jones owes in compensatory damages to Heslin and Lewis, who lost their 6-year-old son in the shooting. Their son was among 20 children and six educators killed in the 2012 attack in Newtown, Conn.

On Friday, Jones said his legal team will continue to appeal the case to the state Supreme Court to get the remaining damages thrown out.

The ruling also does not affect the $1.25 billion Jones still has to pay to other families in Connecticut after he was found to be liable for harassment they endured when he claimed the mass shooting never happened.

The Supreme Court in 2025 turned down Jones’s petition to avoid paying the sum, which had plunged him into bankruptcy.

Jones has yet to make any payments in either state as he continues to appeal the damages amounts and the attempt to liquidate his company, Free Speech Systems (FSS), which oversees Infowars.

The Texas court in May had paused efforts made by satirical outlet The Onion from taking over FSS and Infowars. The deal would have given the outlet temporary authority and use of its trademarks.

Jones has fought to retain control over the company and called the deal “illegal.”

articles.title: GOP raises concerns over Trump lifting certain ground beef tariffs
articles.summary: Welcome to The Hill’s Business & Economy newsletter {beacon} Business & Economy Business & Economy The Big Story GOP backlash grows to Trump beef intervention GOP lawmakers and cattle ranchers are immediately raising alarm bells over President Trump’s decision to temporarily lift certain tariffs on imported ground beef to mitigate the cost for American…
articles.body:
GOP backlash grows to Trump beef intervention

GOP lawmakers and cattle ranchers are immediately raising alarm bells over President Trump’s decision to temporarily lift certain tariffs on imported ground beef to mitigate the cost for American consumers.

The president said Friday a deal is coming that would lower the price of ground beef for Americans to 25 percent below the current market price. It failed to say from which country the beef would be imported.

Critics say that while keeping prices affordable for Americans is important, it shouldn’t be done at the expense of American cattle ranchers.

“While America’s cattle producers share the goal of keeping groceries affordable for consumers, flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd,” Colin Woodall, CEO of the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, said in a statement.

“Cattle markets have already turned sharply lower this morning, to the detriment of farmers and ranchers.”

“This is a critical time of year for cattle producers, as we approach the season where they are making decisions regarding their herds,” he added.

Trump said the temporarily lifted tariffs would last for 90 days to allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported “as we work to rebuild this herd and help our ranchers.”

articles.title: Trump defends beef import plan after GOP blowback
articles.summary: President Trump defended his decision Friday to temporarily suspend higher tariffs on ground beef imports, saying it’s “what the people want.” “We want to get the beef prices down, so we will get them down a little bit,” Trump said before boarding Air Force One to fly to South Carolina. “That’s what people want, that’s…
articles.body:
President Trump defended his decision Friday to temporarily suspend higher tariffs on ground beef imports, saying it’s “what the people want.”

“We want to get the beef prices down, so we will get them down a little bit,” Trump said before boarding Air Force One to fly to South Carolina. “That’s what people want, that’s what the voters want, and that’s what I want.”

“The ranchers are great. They are my people. I love the ranchers; they’ve done a fantastic job,” he added. “But they admit that we need a little help in order to get the prices down, so that is what we’re doing.”

Trump in a social media post earlier Friday announced that he was temporarily lifting certain tariffs on imported ground beef to lower the cost of beef for consumers. The suspension would be for 90 days and would allow up to 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported.

He also said a deal was coming that would lower the price of ground beef to 25 percent below the current market price but didn’t say where the beef would be coming from.

When asked at Joint Base Andrews what countries the deal was with, he said he didn’t want to say.

“There are a few countries, but they’re going to be sending in the highest quality beef, and it’s something that we need,” he said.

Ranchers and GOP lawmakers immediately criticized the president’s announcement.

Colin Woodall, CEO of the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, said in a statement that the association was “disappointed” by the decision.

“While America’s cattle producers share the goal of keeping groceries affordable for consumers, flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd,” Woodall said. “Cattle markets have already turned sharply lower this morning, to the detriment of farmers and ranchers.”

“This is a critical time of year for cattle producers, as we approach the season where they are making decisions regarding their herds,” he added. “Cattle farmers and ranchers are responding to strong market signals and historically high demand, and we are already working to rebuild after years of ongoing drought, high input costs and other challenges that have reduced U.S. cattle numbers.”

He said the announcement throws “cold water” on the idea of expanding herds.

Meriwether Farms, a farm-to-table cattle operation from Wyoming, called the president’s actions a “betrayal” on social media.

Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) said she was “extremely disappointed” with the decision.

“We all want lower grocery prices, but as I’ve said for months, we cannot do it at the expense of American producers,” she wrote on social platform X. “Flooding the market with foreign beef hurts our livestock industry and undermines the long-term solution: growing the U.S. cattle herd to meet demand.”

articles.title: Trump has mountain of Leavitt replacements, says Scott Jennings ‘is good’
articles.summary: President Trump said Friday he’s never seen so many job applications in his life in response to the opening created by Karoline Leavitt’s decision to leave her post as White House press secretary. Asked by reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland about whom he was considering to replace Leavitt, Trump declined to give a…
articles.body:
President Trump said Friday he’s never seen so many job applications in his life in response to the opening created by Karoline Leavitt’s decision to leave her post as White House press secretary.

Asked by reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland about whom he was considering to replace Leavitt , Trump declined to give a name but signaled the choice could be difficult.

Pointing to different reporters standing on the tarmac with him, Trump said, “I don’t know, maybe you.”

“I will tell you this, and Karoline will tell you this, I have never seen so many job applications in my life,” he added.

Leavitt, who was standing next to Trump, nodded in agreement, saying “there’s a lot of options.”

The president continued that Leavitt “made that job very glamorous” so “they all want that job; they love that job.”

A reporter asked him if CNN political commentator Scott Jennings was being considered for the position.

“Scott Jennings is good,” the president responded.

Jennings, who has worked on two campaigns for former President George W. Bush and served as an adviser to Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), has been CNN’s primary conservative analyst since 2017. He was reportedly being considered for the position in 2024 following Trump’s election win.

In an Aug. 13 appearance on “CNN NewsNight,” Jennings told other panelists that he did not know if he would replace Leavitt.

“But I’ll tell you this: Karoline Leavitt has been maybe the greatest White House press secretary in the last 30 years, at least. She’s been nothing short of brilliant,” he stated. “I don’t know a single Republican in the country who isn’t in awe of and in appreciation of Karoline tonight.”

Leavitt said she was leaving the job to care for her two young children.

“I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House press secretary,” she said earlier this month.

She has been Trump’s only press secretary in his second term. During Trump’s first term, Sean Spicer, now-Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), Stephanie Grisham and Kayleigh McEnany served in the role.

articles.title: Watch live: Trump stumps for Darline Graham in South Carolina
articles.summary: President Trump will hit the campaign trail Friday in South Carolina to rally support for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) ahead of the state’s Republican runoff next week, when she’s set to face off against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.). Trump’s appearance comes as Graham faces scrutiny for a rough debate performance earlier this week, after which…
articles.body:
President Trump will hit the campaign trail Friday in South Carolina to rally support for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) ahead of the state’s Republican runoff next week, when she’s set to face off against Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.).

Trump’s appearance comes as Graham faces scrutiny for a rough debate performance earlier this week, after which she was slammed over her lack of knowledge on national security issues.

Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), was appointed last month by GOP Gov. Henry McMaster to fill out the remainder of her brother’s term. The political newcomer is relying heavily on the president’s endorsement to keep her seat in the upper chamber.

Prominent Palmetto State Republicans, many of whom also vied for the spot, are split between Graham and Norman. Rep. Russell Fry, who finished third in the initial primary , has backed the incumbent , while former Gov. Mark Sanford (R) has endorsed her challenger . The campaign stop will be in Myrtle Beach, S.C., which falls in Fry’s 7th Congressional District.

The event is scheduled to begin at 7 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: Interior Department outlines short-term plan for water cuts in California, Arizona, Nevada
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story DOI outlines short-term plan for water cuts in CA, AZ, NV The federal government has unveiled its short-term plans for Colorado River water cuts from California, Arizona and Nevada — issuing a plan that’s largely in line with what the states themselves have proposed…
articles.body:
DOI outlines short-term plan for water cuts in CA, AZ, NV

The federal government has unveiled its short-term plans for Colorado River water cuts from California, Arizona and Nevada — issuing a plan that’s largely in line with what the states themselves have proposed and sparing them from more dramatic cuts for the time being.

The Interior Department announced Friday that it would require these states, collectively known as the Lower Basin states, to reduce their water use by 1.25 million acre-feet per year in 2027 and 2028.

It encourages them to conserve and store an additional 700,000 acre-feet in total over the next two years.

That lines up with a plan put forward by the three states in which they suggested they could cut 1.25 million acre-feet over the same period.

The short-term guidelines follow the federal government’s recent announcement of a 10-year framework in which it said the states could be forced to cut as much as 3 million acre-feet per year.

State officials recoiled at the 3 million figure, with Arizona and Nevada officials saying cuts that steep could devastate local economies . Interior has said that the 10-year plan is meant to be flexible and responsive to whatever the water conditions may be down the road — meaning the states may never actually see cuts that are that steep.

The department also said Friday that it was finalizing its 10-year framework decision that includes the potentially steeper water cuts.

articles.title: Rising data center backlash shakes up 2026 races
articles.summary: {beacon} Technology Technology The Big Story Rising data center backlash shakes up 2026 races As public pushback to data centers boils over, politicians on both sides of the aisle are racing to distance themselves from the controversial facilities. © Adobe Stock Key swing state candidates are scrambling to endorse stricter data center policies and…
articles.body:
Rising data center backlash shakes up 2026 races

As public pushback to data centers boils over, politicians on both sides of the aisle are racing to distance themselves from the controversial facilities.

Key swing state candidates are scrambling to endorse stricter data center policies and accusing their opponents of being too cozy with the industry, as Americans become increasingly hostile to the rapid buildout of AI infrastructure.

articles.title: Trump says he’ll spend ‘a lot’ of MAGA Inc. funds in midterms
articles.summary: President Trump said he’s prepared to spend “a lot” of money from his MAGA Inc. campaign account to support Republican candidates this midterm cycle. “Well, I’ve raised a lot, and nobody knows what it is, but I will tell you it’s about $850 million,” Trump said before boarding Air Force One to fly to South…
articles.body:
President Trump said he’s prepared to spend “a lot” of money from his MAGA Inc. campaign account to support Republican candidates this midterm cycle.

“Well, I’ve raised a lot, and nobody knows what it is, but I will tell you it’s about $850 million,” Trump said before boarding Air Force One to fly to South Carolina. “I’ll be spending a lot of that money for — and my own money — but I’ll be spending a lot of that money for candidates that I think are good, Republican candidates.”

Election forecasters favor Democrats to win the House and give Republicans a slight edge in the Senate race, though momentum is moving against the GOP, due largely to Trump’s sinking approval and the Iran war.

MAGA Inc. is a super PAC that heavily supported Trump’s 2024 campaign.

Trump said earlier this month in an interview with Punchbowl News that he could “spend it on pretty much anything” he wants.

“I’m going to help Republicans,” he said.

So far, the super PAC hasn’t spent any money on candidates in June or July.

Some Republicans told Politico last month that they wish the president would start opening up the coffers to help GOP candidates.

James Blair, a top Trump political adviser who oversees the super PAC, said the president “is going to expend substantial resources to win the midterms.”

“He cares deeply about the party winning and anything he can do to support that he is going to do and is already doing,” Blair said on “The Sean Spicer Show” in June.

He wouldn’t say when the money would be sent, only that it would be “very soon.”

articles.title: Trump defends Darline Graham’s Taiwan response: ‘She was being honest’
articles.summary: President Trump defended Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Friday following her stumble on a national security question during the Palmetto State’s GOP Senate primary debate this week. The president offered his support to Graham as he was on his way to Myrtle Beach, S.C., where he’s set to rally alongside her Friday evening, just days…
articles.body:
President Trump defended Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Friday following her stumble on a national security question during the Palmetto State’s GOP Senate primary debate this week.

The president offered his support to Graham as he was on his way to Myrtle Beach, S.C., where he’s set to rally alongside her Friday evening, just days ahead of the state’s Republican runoff.

Trump has consistently endorsed Graham, especially during her face off against Rep. Ralph Norman (S.C.), since she was appointed to fill out the rest of her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham’s (R-S.C.) term.

“She’s very smart, and she was being honest. She’s into the price of groceries. … She is going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants,” Trump said Friday before leaving for South Carolina.

“She understands that national security is my thing. … I thought it was a very honest answer,” the president continued.

Darline Graham’s slip up earlier this week has raised concerns over whether she is too much of a political novice to fill her brother’s role, who served in the Air Force and had extensive national security experience.

When asked at the debate if Taiwan and the South China Sea are national security issues for the U.S., Darline Graham responded, “I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not that informed on national security.”

Following the debate, she acknowledged her mistake, telling Fox News on Wednesday that she “tripped up” on her answer.

“I have said many times I’m not a politician, certainly not a career politician. I don’t speak politician,” Graham continued as part of her defense.

Former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley (R) was among those who criticized Graham’s response, saying the late senator’s sister is not qualified to keep her post for a full term.

“Lindsey Graham was well informed on the United States’ national security. Darline Graham admits she’s not,” Haley wrote Tuesday on the social platform X . “This is not something you inherit. And it’s critical in the U.S. Senate.”

Norman, Graham’s challenger, also received an endorsement from former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford (R) on Friday — despite him usually refraining from backing political candidates. Sanford finished fourth in the Senate GOP primary in June.

The president will campaign Friday night with Graham in Myrtle Beach, a key district in the state and home to former Senate candidate Rep. Russell Fry (R-S.C.). As Fry did not advance to the GOP runoff, Norman and Graham may see his 7th Congressional District as a way to reach new audiences.

South Carolina’s Republican primary runoff will be held Tuesday.

articles.title: Log Cabin Republicans cut ties with transgender movement
articles.summary: The Log Cabin Republicans (LCR) announced Thursday that it would halt its support for the transgender community, calling itself an “LGB advocacy organization.” LCR President Ross Hemminger wrote in an op-ed published to the conservative outlet “Townhall” that the move signaled an adjustment to its “national advocacy focus,” saying the organization wanted to distance itself…
articles.body:
The Log Cabin Republicans (LCR) announced Thursday that it would halt its support for the transgender community, calling itself an “LGB advocacy organization.”

LCR President Ross Hemminger wrote in an op-ed published to the conservative outlet “Townhall” that the move signaled an adjustment to its “national advocacy focus,” saying the organization wanted to distance itself from transgender activists — who he claimed fostered an “unnecessary and discomfiting focus on America’s youth.”

The group, centered around gay conservatives and their allies, added transgender people to its mission in 2015, according to Hemminger’s op-ed. LCR previously used the acronym “LGBT” — short for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender — on its website but has since removed the “t” from such references.

“We are an LGB advocacy organization,” he wrote, “as our founders envisioned and as our moral center calls us to be.”

Hemminger added that the move was in response to what the organization believed were pushes by the transgender community to “teach radical gender ideology” and put “biological men in women’s sports regardless of the consequences.”

“Most offensively, they support gender reassignment treatments for minors, often without the knowledge or consent of the parents,” Hemminger continued. “Their view of the gay community is based on today’s radical transgender activists with their unnecessary and discomfiting focus on America’s youth.”

He went on to clarify that the decision does not disqualify anyone from affiliating themselves with the organization, adding that membership “remains open to all conservatives.”

LCR has chapters in more than 40 states and claims to be the nation’s largest and oldest organization serving LBG conservatives, according to its website.

The decision to exclude transgender people from its mission follows a Supreme Court decision allowing states to bar transgender athletes from certain sports. Nearly 30 states have instituted laws since the decision.

These debates have extended to sport governing bodies, with the NCAA similarly banning transgender athletes from the women’s category in 2025 — while men’s categories are still open to all eligible student-athletes. Recently, the WNBA has faced backlash from conservatives for some players’ and staffs’ support of transgender athletes.

“The new era of gender identity politics is not the movement (LCR) supported and fought for,” Hellinger wrote.

articles.title: Trump eyes vaccine categories
articles.summary: Click in for more news from The Hill {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story Trump eyes vaccine categories To support President Trump’s vaccine executive order issued earlier this month, the administration is considering to changing or adding to the categories of vaccinations, in what critics argue is another effort by the White House to…
articles.body:
To support President Trump’s vaccine executive order issued earlier this month, the administration is considering to changing or adding to the categories of vaccinations , in what critics argue is another effort by the White House to undermine existing vaccine policies.

A Request for Information (RFI) filed on Friday by the Department of Health and Human Service (HHS) asks for public comment on whether current federal categories for vaccinations are “adequate.”

Vaccines are categorized as routine (universal), risk-based or shared clinical decision-making (SCDM).

“The Department seeks comment on these categories and whether additional or different categories should be adopted,” the RFI states.

As the document notes, SCDM was adopted by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in 2019. SCDM applies to vaccines are those that a provider and patient can discuss and decide whether they would have benefits for that individual .

In his executive order earlier this month, Trump called for moving certain childhood vaccines from being universal to being either risk-based or SCDM, reducing the number of routine immunizations from 18 to 11 .

Health care attorney Richard Hughes IV blasted the RFI in a memo Friday.

“Whether or not the development of the SCDM category is considered beneficial, considerable ACIP deliberation went into its creation. Under the guise of simply requesting information, the administration is now making clear its intent to modify existing recommendation categories, or even create new ones,” wrote Hughes.

“Perhaps even more troubling is what the RFI does not say. It makes no mention of ACIP, the body charged with developing vaccine recommendations since 1964, whose recommendations are the indispensable legal trigger for ACA coverage mandates, VFC program scope, EPSDT obligations, Medicare Part D zero-cost-sharing, and pharmacist scope-of-practice authority across dozens of states,” he added.

The public can submit comments until September 20, 2026 .

articles.title: White House rips Rosie O’Donnell for Trump, Harp jokes: She’s ‘a total slob’
articles.summary: The White House responded Thursday to comments made by comedian Rosie O’Donnell while hosting “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” concerning President Trump and his administration. Davis Ingle, a representative for the White House, said in a statement to news outlets that “Rosie O’Donnell is a nasty woman and a total slob whose brain has been completely destroyed…
articles.body:
The White House responded Thursday to comments made by comedian Rosie O’Donnell while hosting “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” concerning President Trump and his administration.

Davis Ingle, a representative for the White House, said in a statement to news outlets that “Rosie O’Donnell is a nasty woman and a total slob whose brain has been completely destroyed by Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

O’Donnell hosted the program for three days where she made nods in her opening monologues to the president, referring to him as “orange Voldemort” in her final broadcast Thursday before performing a song.

articles.title: President makes final push for Darline Graham in trip to ‘Trump country’
articles.summary: Myrtle Beach, S.C. — President Trump travelled south to rally support for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Friday ahead of next week’s primary runoff and urged Republicans to turn out in November’s midterm elections. “I think Lindsey respected Darline more than any other person he knows including me, and that does not make me happy,”…
articles.body:
Myrtle Beach, S.C. — President Trump travelled south to rally support for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) on Friday ahead of next week’s primary runoff and urged Republicans to turn out in November’s midterm elections.

“I think Lindsey respected Darline more than any other person he knows including me, and that does not make me happy,” Trump quipped, referring to Graham’s late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died last month.

Graham joined Trump on stage at one point during rally, declaring “this is Trump country.”

The president hit South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews without naming her, labeling her as “far left.

He did name Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, who are both locked in close races with Trump-backed GOP candidates.

The president also sought to use the rally to push Republican turnout in November.

“We have to make the midterm elections too big to rig,” he said, alluding to his frequent and unfounded claims of election fraud.

The president acknowledged issues Republicans face in turning out their base when he is not at the top of the ballot.

“What I want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” he said.

Trump also warned supporters that Democrats will move to impeach him if Republicans lose their majorities in Congress.

“I’m going to be impeached. They’re going to impeach me. They have no idea why,” he said.

The president addressed non-campaign related issues as well.

He took the opportunity to celebrate the Supreme Court’s ruling on Friday that allowed construction on the White House ballroom to continue, at least until the appeal receives a full review.

“I’m in a very good mood tonight,” Trump said, referring to news of the ruling.

Trump also declared that he views the Strait of Hormuz as a U.S. territory after saying last week he wanted to annex the waterway. Trump has shifted from military strikes to threats of economic isolation in his push to force concessions from Tehran.

The primary runoff marks a major test for Trump’s endorsement as Graham, a political newcomer temporarily appointed to her brother’s seat, runs to keep it for another six years. She is facing off against Rep. Ralph Norman, a real estate developer elected to the House in 2017.

Graham made headlines earlier this week at a televised debate with Norman when she flubbed a question on Taiwan and the South China Sea, saying national security was not her thing.

The answer was a sea change between her and her late brother, who was known as a foreign policy giant in the Senate. It was also met with immediate criticism from Norman and his allies.

Trump defended Graham’s response to the question ahead of his trip to South Carolina on Friday.

“She’s very smart, and she was being honest. She’s into the price of groceries. … She is going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants,” Trump said before boarding Air Force One.

“She understands that national security is my thing. … I thought it was a very honest answer,” he continued.

Graham enters the primary with an advantage from Trump’s endorsement and her status as Lindsey Graham’s sister. Trump won the state by nearly 18 points in 2024, by 11 points in 2020, and by 14 points in 2016.

The winner of Tuesday’s runoff will run against Andrews.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the state’s Senate race as solid Republican, but nationally Republicans are facing headwinds amid Trump’s declining approval ratings and rising Democratic enthusiasm.

Trump’s approval rating in South Carolina sits at 42 percent, according to a Civiqs tracking poll .

articles.title: Leavitt to work at Trump-affiliated super PAC following White House departure
articles.summary: Karoline Leavitt is set to work at President Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC following her departure from the White House, the outgoing press secretary confirmed Friday. Leavitt shared her next career move with reporters outside of Air Force One Friday evening, a little over one week after she announced she would step down at the…
articles.body:
Karoline Leavitt is set to work at President Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC following her departure from the White House , the outgoing press secretary confirmed Friday.

Leavitt shared her next career move with reporters outside of Air Force One Friday evening, a little over one week after she announced she would step down at the end of August to spend more time with her family.

She did not elaborate on what her title would be a MAGA Inc. — a Trump and GOP-aligned PAC reportedly sitting on over $350 million in campaign funds ahead of November’s midterms. Leavitt served as a spokesperson for the PAC before joining the president’s 2024 campaign.

“You guys will still see me all the time,” the outgoing press secretary told reporters Friday.

Leavitt also added that the Friday evening flight — a trip to Myrtle Beach, S.C. for a Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) rally featuring the president — would be her last official outing as press secretary.

After Leavitt announced her departure, Trump said she would continue working with the White House as one of his “top advisers” and be an “influential voice within the Republican Party.” The press secretary herself said in her announcement that her “fight” against the Democratic Party would not end once she vacated the post.

The White House notably did not name an immediate replacement for Leavitt, who had returned from maternity leave in mid-July shortly before deciding to permanently leave the role. Trump commented on mounting speculation surrounding who would be her replacement, signaling that he had several options and that the choice would be difficult.

“I will tell you this, and Karoline will tell you this, I have never seen so many job applications in my life,” Trump told reporters Friday.

Top contenders for the role reportedly include CNN conservative commentator Scott Jennings and Katie Miller, the wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, among others.

Although Leavitt confirmed the Myrtle Beach rally would be her last event serving as press secretary, she said Friday that she still planned to join the president throughout the midterms campaign trail, including at September’s GOP convention in Dallas.

articles.title: ‘Shocking’ fake poll firm puts industry under the microscope: ‘Unfortunately not surprising’
articles.summary: The revelation that two polls released in recent weeks from a purported polling firm were faked is adding a new curveball for a polling industry already trying to improve public trust in its work. Median Strategies made the stunning announcement earlier this past week that its poll results of the Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary and the Los Angeles mayoral race were not real and…
articles.body:
The revelation that two polls released in recent weeks from a purported polling firm were faked is adding a new curveball for a polling industry already trying to improve public trust in its work.

Median Strategies made the stunning announcement earlier this past week that its poll results of the Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary and the Los Angeles mayoral race were not real and instead were put out as part of a “social experiment.” It said they should not be cited or treated as legitimate data.

Coming off well-publicized polling misses in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary and the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, the timing of the ploy wasn’t helpful either.

Pollsters said this incident emphasizes the due diligence that media outlets and the public must conduct when looking at and trying to understand numbers being released.

“It was very shocking, but unfortunately not surprising,” Ben Leff, the CEO of the polling and survey research firm Verasight, said about Median’s fake polls. “I think the industry and media are used to probably polls that aren’t conducted very well in terms of rigorous methods or how they’re verifying respondents, but this was sort of the extreme of that, where everything was completely fake.”

The polling industry has already been dealing for years with struggles to improve its credibility in the eyes of the public, with trust shaken by President Trump’s repeated outperformances in 2016, 2020 and 2024, to varying extents .

But that has been at least based on good-faith efforts from pollsters trying to model what an election may look like the best they can. That’s a different situation from Median, which pollsters emphasized shouldn’t be considered part of the industry.

Median first released a poll on the Los Angeles mayor’s race, a contest that hasn’t seen any major public polling conducted since the primary election in June. It showed Mayor Karen Bass (D) leading progressive City Council member Nithya Raman (D) by 12 points, a lead that Bass touted in a later-deleted post on the social platform X.

After Median revealed the poll was fake, Bass’s campaign denounced it, with a spokesperson calling for any “bad faith attempts to influence elections” to be “investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

Raman’s campaign attacked Bass for promoting a “fake poll without properly vetting the source.”

A second fake poll from Median showed Wisconsin state Rep. Francesca Hong leading the state’s Democratic primary for governor by 20 points. The democratic socialist ultimately lost the primary earlier this month in a major upset .

The poll’s result was largely in line with what several other polls from legitimate firms were indicating, though polling was limited in the primary race’s final weeks.

The extent to which the poll influenced expectations, and potentially turnout in the race, is impossible to quantify, but the more immediate impact may be how polls are perceived as the country is gearing up for the critical midterm elections in November.

Geoffrey Skelley, the chief elections analyst at Decision Desk HQ, noted the impact is different than if a major pollster was revealed to be falsifying data. But he said he understands how this could affect perception.

“I understand why, say in the aftermath of 2016, people have that attitude,” he said. “That is concerning, that it sort of adds fuel to the fire of ‘The polls are worthless,’ ‘The polls are meaningless,’ ‘They’re not even real’-kind of conversation.”

Median maintained on its website that it wanted to see what would happen if it put out fake polls.

“Median Strategies was created as a short-term social experiment examining how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification,” its message read.

Median did not return a request from The Hill for comment.

The Guardian identified the source behind Median as 21-year-old Rahil Prakash, a recent college graduate. He said he was inspired by the polling miss in the Michigan Senate primary to see if fake polls could “penetrate the ecosystem” easily.

“I was a bit shocked, perhaps at how fast this sort of information can spread,” he said.

Prakash said he wanted to apologize to the Bass, Raman and Hong campaigns.

“And I hope it gives a really good lesson going forward in that we need to be very serious about these things and very serious in how, if one person can do this, what can a serious operation do in the future,” he said.

Experts expressed skepticism about Median’s claims about its motive, noting various political or financial incentives for the results. The rise of prediction markets in recent years gives another potential impact on this, as bettors place wagers on a wide range of questions, including on who will win an election. Prakash told The Guardian he placed no bets on the races.

Skelley said fake pollsters have put out results in the past intended to influence prediction markets and make money off the impacts. But they have generally not come off looking as legitimate as Median did, either not having a website or having a suspicious-looking one.

Leff said the first step that media outlets and members of the public should do if they see a poll from a pollster they don’t recognize is check if the pollster is a member of the American Association for Public Opinion Research’s Transparency Initiative .

He said the initiative is similar to the bar for attorneys and provides credentials to pollsters that are transparent about disclosing their methodologies in detail.

He said a second step is looking for a detailed methodology statement provided to the public included in the poll’s release. That statement would include information such as the number of respondents, margin of error and how respondents were recruited.

Leff said Median had a “top-line” report of its methodology that didn’t provide a lot of details.

“That was immediately a red flag to us,” he said.

Of course, even a detailed methodology statement could still be faked, and conducting a deep dive may be more extensive than the average person knows to do or takes the time for.

John Cluverius, the director of survey research for the UMass Lowell Center for Public Opinion, said this underscores the importance of not giving too much emphasis to any single poll but what pictures various polls from different pollsters are painting.

“Thinking about polls in terms of them being different snapshots that are trying to measure the same thing, I think that’s very useful,” he said.

Cluverius said he believes media outlets have become “smarter” about insisting on transparency from polling firms, becoming more selective in which polls they cover and don’t, which can help weed out those that are faulty.

Leff noted this is just one of the threats the polling industry faces, pointing to bots and artificial intelligence that attempt to take surveys.

In another incident, the polling aggregator FiftyPlusOne announced Thursday that it would “permanently ban” one polling firm and suspend another over a lack of disclosure that Florida GOP gubernatorial candidate James Fishback’s campaign was funding them. The banned firm was also accused of fabricating data, a claim that it denies.

Ryan O’Donnell, the executive director of the left-leaning pollster Data for Progress, said the takeaway from the controversy needs to be more vigilance.

“The lesson here isn’t that we should stop trusting polling — understanding public opinion is vital to a functioning democracy and there are plenty of credible, trustworthy pollsters out there,” he said. “People just need to know what to look for.”

articles.title: DHS starts deportation flights after end to remaining protections for TPS holders
articles.summary: Lower court judges have now fully lifted certain limitations on the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in the wake of a Supreme Court decision that cleared the end of temporary protected status (TPS), removing any final roadblock to deportations. A federal judge earlier this week lifted the final stay that barred immigration officials from carrying…
articles.body:
Lower court judges have now fully lifted certain limitations on the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in the wake of a Supreme Court decision that cleared the end of temporary protected status (TPS), removing any final roadblock to deportations.

A federal judge earlier this week lifted the final stay that barred immigration officials from carrying out deportations to Ethiopia. That was the last of various court cases by TPS recipients challenging the termination of their protections.

Immigration officials are now free to deport nationals from 13 countries that prior administrations determined were not sufficiently stable because of natural disaster or civil unrest to safely return migrants.

The additional four countries that still retain their TPS designation are set to expire shortly, meaning more than 1.3 million protectees either have or are likely to soon lose their legal status.

“Effectively, this signals the end of the program,” Nayna Gupta, policy director at the American Immigration Council, told The Hill.

“This an unprecedented delegalization campaign. It’s the largest effort to strip people of lawful status in U.S. history.”

The Supreme Court in its June ruling didn’t end the TPS program but determined the courts did not have the power to review the administration’s decision to end protections for citizens of Haiti and Syria — two countries marred by violence.

While that left very narrow grounds to continue litigation, the ruling has real-life impact now.

Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance, a nonprofit advocacy group that also provides legal services to TPS holders, shared the story of one Haitian woman who fled to the U.S. at age 19.

“For the first time when she got to the United States, she woke up and was not worried about being kidnapped by armed groups in Haiti. For the first time, she wasn’t worried about seeing a dead body on the street of where she lived. For the first time, she went to bed not hearing gunshots,” Jozef said.

“After the termination of TPS, when she saw an ICE car for the first time she felt so unsafe again, fearful that she would be taken by ICE, so the same fear that she had about being kidnapped by armed groups in Haiti came back in the form of being kidnapped by ICE,” she said, using an abbreviation for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Beyond Haiti and Syria, TPS holders from Venezuela, Nicaragua, Honduras, Afghanistan, Cameroon, Nepal, South Sudan, Burma, Ethiopia, Yemen and Somalia can now be deported.

Lower courts had blocked DHS from carrying out deportations, but those rulings had to be reexamined in the wake of the high court’s ruling, even though many judges had initially sided with TPS holders in temporarily blocking deportations.

James Percival, the top attorney at DHS, celebrated when the final stay was lifted by a lower court judge based in Massachusetts.

“Judge Brian Murphy just lifted the stay of Ethiopia TPS termination. All TPS terminations are in effect!” he wrote Tuesday on the social platform X, sharing a graphic modeled after one used by Facebook that allows users to mark themselves as safe after an event, with the attorney writing he was now safe “from TPS judges today.”

Haitians are among the largest groups of TPS holders, with nearly 350,000 protected under the status prior to the Supreme Court ruling.

Many are now contemplating what to do next as their once-legal status evaporates.

“It’s been an incredibly difficult, painful time,” said Jozef, who added that it comes after “a difficult day, week, month, and year.”

On Thursday night, the Trump administration conducted its first deportation flight to Haiti since the end of TPS, a plane Jozef said carried roughly 170 people, including one of her clients.

Many TPS holders are now being pressured to return to countries where the State Department has actively highlighted the dangers on the ground.

That’s particularly true for Haiti and Syria.

The Caribbean nation has been dominated by gang violence in the wake of an assassination of their prime minister in 2021 that has left the country with a transitional government.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fla.) visited Haiti earlier this summer as part of a congressional delegation, describing the country as having areas “like Afghanistan” — where he was deployed while in the military — and adding “it is probably the poorest place I’ve ever been through in my life.”

In Syria, warring factions are still feuding across the country after ousting leader Bashar Assad, who deployed chemical weapons against his own people.

The State Department has rated each a “Level 4 Do Not Travel” country.

The Haiti deportation flight carried out Thursday night landed in the northern coastal city of Cap-Haitien, as the U.S. bars commercial flights into Port-au-Prince — where gang members who largely control the capital city routinely fire at landing planes.

Jozef noted a high-ranking military leader, charged with protecting the public, was ironically kidnapped earlier this summer by gangs.

“If the department that is in charge of protecting the people, they themselves have been kidnapped, how will they be able to protect people being deported to Haiti right now?” she asked.

“Even the Department of Defense is unable to defend themselves against the armed groups in Haiti right now.”

Many judges made it clear the Supreme Court had tied their hands after they issued rulings backing TPS holders on a number of grounds, including that the Trump administration had acted with racial animus in terminating the protections.

Massachusetts-based U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs wrote an emotional order last week lifting her earlier block on deporting citizens of Somalia.

“Plaintiffs have made a convincing showing that they will suffer irreparable harm if the injunction is withheld … and the balance of hardships and the public interest also favor Plaintiffs, given that the government has made no showing that maintaining TPS status for the duration of this litigation would impose an undue burden,” she wrote.

Also frightening for TPS holders is they have little control over where they may be deported. While some might be returned to their home countries, TPS holders could be sent to a third country if their home nation doesn’t accept flights. Eswatini and Liberia are among those that have agreed to accept deportees.

Jozef noted that many times, those sent to third countries are often placed in “confinement” in a prisonlike setting.

“The deportations are costing U.S. taxpayers money — it is not free,” she said, noting that the U.S. has agreed to pay other countries millions to accept deportees.

And though not a TPS holder, one deportee sent to Haiti was from the Dominican Republic, according to The Associated Press .

Thursday night’s deportation flight, while not the first to Haiti, represents the beginning of an expected uptick in such removals, particularly for TPS holders.

Gupta noted that plan is not without challenges in countries like Haiti, “where conditions are so horrific on the ground that it’s difficult for airplanes to land in the country,” meaning the Trump administration “is likely facing greater logistical barriers on that front.”

Jozef noted that many TPS holders, particularly from countries that have been more recently designated, have few options for attaining some other form of legal status. Many do not have U.S. citizen children who have reached age 21, where they would be able to sponsor them to adjust their status.

“There are a lot of people who have applied for asylum. Unfortunately, 90 percent of those cases have been denied,” she said.

Gupta and other immigration advocates have for years advocated for TPS holders to be able to obtain a permanent path to citizenship, but like many immigration efforts in Congress, those pushes have stalled.

“While it is absolutely shocking because it violates American norms,” she said of the TPS deportations, “it’s unsurprising in that we knew this was always a risk, and that these were folks who are always vulnerable, given their liminal status, which inherently means not having a permanent place here in the United States.”

articles.title: Live updates: Carney suspends trade talks with US, Freedom 250 Grand Prix begins in Washington
articles.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced on social platform X that the country would be suspending its trade talks with the U.S., setting Trump’s 50 percent tariffs into motion. “The U.S. intends to impose a 50% tariff on $28 billion of Canadian goods. Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers…
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced on social platform X that the country would be suspending its trade talks with the U.S., setting Trump’s 50 percent tariffs into motion.

“The U.S. intends to impose a 50% tariff on $28 billion of Canadian goods. Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and business,” Carney wrote in a statement Friday night.

The response comes after President Trump’s decision on Thursday night to pause the 50 percent tariffs for three days, saying the U.S. and Canada were finalizing a deal. But Carney believes the trade talks with the U.S. have “not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians.”

Back in Washington, the streets will be filled with the roars of professional motor sports this weekend as the IndyCar Series brings its high-speed show to the nation’s capital for the first time ever for the Freedom 250 Grand Prix.

The event, which spans two days, will close streets near the National Mall and downtown D.C., and marks a dramatic conclusion to the summer’s 250th anniversary celebrations.
